Boston neighborhoods

Massachusetts' capital and largest city sits in Suffolk County. Its Office of Neighborhood Services recognizes 23 neighborhoods, and where your house is matters more to a buyer than the word Boston.

Part of the cityNeighborhoods
Downtown coreDowntown or Financial District, Beacon Hill, West End, North End, Chinatown, Bay Village
Central and waterfrontBack Bay, South End, Seaport District, South Boston, East Boston, Charlestown
West and southwestAllston, Brighton, Fenway-Kenmore, Mission Hill, Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, West Roxbury, Hyde Park
SouthRoxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan

The city has 53 ZIP codes, so check the ZIP and the neighborhood on your assessment record instead of assuming they match.

Housing stock and density

Boston was settled in 1625 and became a city in 1822. More than two thirds of inner Boston's modern land did not exist at the founding. It was made by filling tidal areas. That history shows in the houses: Back Bay has single family homes and wooden and brick multi-family row houses, the South End Historic District is the largest surviving contiguous Victorian era neighborhood in the country, and downtown and South Boston mix low rise masonry buildings with modern towers.

If your house is in a historic district such as the South End, ask the city whether review rules apply to exterior work before you plan any repairs.

Boston is the most densely populated state capital in the country, at about 13,977 people per square mile of land. Around 1.2 million people may be inside city limits during work hours. For a seller, on-street parking, building access and noise are real selling points or objections, and buyers will ask about them on a walkthrough.

Weather and your building

Boston has hot, humid summers and cold, stormy winters, with occasional periods of heavy snow. The freezing window runs from about November 9 to April 5. Winters can bring wide swings, and the immediate coast often sees rain where inland areas see snow. Expect buyers to ask about the roof, windows and heating. Brick and masonry buildings with old mortar, and wooden row houses with aging porches, show weather damage in different ways, so a recent repair record helps you answer questions. If you have invoices for roof or heating work, keep them with your other sale paperwork.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Boston house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Property tax and abatements

Values are set as of January 1 before the fiscal year. If you think yours is too high, the first move is an abatement application to the city's assessors. It is due by the date the first actual tax bill comes due, which is generally February 1 where billing is quarterly.

Appeals go next to the Appellate Tax Board, which sits at 100 Cambridge Street at Government Center and often hears cases by video. A typical single family hearing lasts one to two hours, and getting to one can take four months to a year.

Call the Boston Assessing Department for the current rate, to ask whether your home qualifies for the residential exemption, and to confirm your abatement deadline. Your actual bill states the due dates.

Closing a Boston sale

Suffolk County Registry of Deeds records your deed, since Boston is in Suffolk County. A deed excise tax is charged at recording. Norfolk County's registry lists $2.28 per $500 of the price or fraction of it, and the same state statute covers Suffolk, so get the Suffolk fee schedule from the registry or your attorney.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. The fire department issues a certificate of compliance. Book the inspection the day a closing date is set, and expect a fee.
  • Attorney. Lender-side closings need an attorney's real involvement, which is why most sales use a real estate attorney.
  • Home inspection. Under 760 CMR 74, a seller of certain residential properties cannot make an offer depend on the buyer waiving an inspection.
  • Title systems. Most parcels are recorded land. A few are registered land with a Land Court certificate.

The Secretary of the Commonwealth runs a notification service that emails you when a document is recorded against your property. It is useful for an inherited home or any house with a title question.

Selling a house with tenants

Plenty of Boston houses hold more than one unit. If yours does, the city's Inspectional Services Department can tell you whether the building must be registered or inspected as a rental, and your attorney can explain how leases pass to a buyer.

A direct sale lets you skip showings while tenants stay in place. Cash Home Buyers buys Boston houses as they are, and you can compare our number with a listing price before you decide.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Boston houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Preparing the paperwork

Most delays in a Boston sale come from documents, not buyers. Start with the ones only you can find: the deed, your latest tax bill, any permit records for work done on the house, and a list of repairs you know about. If a relative owned the house before you, add the probate paperwork. If tenants live there, add every lease.

Then check what the city already has. The Assessing Department can tell you how your property is classified and whether a residential exemption is on file. Inspectional Services can tell you about rental registration. The registry holds the recorded history of your title, and the notification service mentioned above will tell you if anything new is filed against it.

Put the contacts and answers in one folder. Your attorney and any buyer, cash or otherwise, will ask for the same items, and having them ready shortens the days between an agreement and a closing.

Why sell as-is in Boston

Older Boston houses often need work that a mortgage lender will flag, such as roofs, heating, wiring or egress. Fixing them before a listing costs money and time, and parking, access and noise already test a buyer's patience. Selling as-is to Cash Home Buyers puts that work on us. You still handle the tax payoff, the alarm certificate and the deed recording, but you skip staging, open houses and a buyer's financing contingency.

Getting ready: a short checklist

  1. Find your latest tax bill and note its due dates and any exemption on it.
  2. Call the Assessing Department about your abatement deadline and the residential exemption.
  3. Confirm your neighborhood and ZIP on the assessment record.
  4. Schedule the fire department certificate once a closing date is set.
  5. Choose a real estate attorney and ask about the Suffolk registry fees.
  6. Gather your mortgage statement, if one remains, so the payoff can be confirmed before closing day.
  7. Ask your attorney who will pay for the fire department inspection, you or the buyer, and put the answer in writing.
  8. If tenants live there, gather the leases and ask Inspectional Services about rental registration.

With a traditional sale, a buyer's lender adds an appraisal and a loan approval to this list. A cash sale drops them, and the house is bought in its current condition.

Frequently asked questions

How many neighborhoods does Boston have?

The city's Office of Neighborhood Services designates 23, including Back Bay, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, South Boston and the North End.

What county is Boston in?

Suffolk County. Deeds for Boston property are recorded at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds.

How do I appeal my Boston property tax assessment?

Start with an abatement application to the Boston assessors, due by the first actual bill's due date. A denial or no answer gives you three months to go to the Appellate Tax Board.

Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell a Boston house?

Yes, for a one or two family home. The local fire department must certify that your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale rules.

Can I sell a Boston house that has tenants?

Yes. Ask Inspectional Services whether the building must be registered or inspected as a rental, and ask your attorney how the leases transfer to a buyer.

Worcester at a glance

Central Massachusetts counts Worcester as its main city. It is the county seat, roughly 40 miles from Boston and 38 from Providence. Residents numbered 206,518 in 2020, and the latest estimate is 213,862, second in the state behind Boston. Route 146 and Interstates 90, 190, 290, 395 and 495 pass through, so commute time is often on a buyer's mind when they tour a house here.

With that many homes changing hands, yours will be compared against plenty of others. Age, condition and street access move the price more than most owners expect.

Triple-deckers and older housing

Worcester's streets were laid out around canals, railways and mills, and the houses show it. Triple-deckers and Victorian-era buildings from the 19th century are everywhere. Factory work shrank after World War II, then healthcare, colleges and biotechnology pulled the population back up beginning in the 1990s.

  • Many buyers see a triple-decker as a small rental business, so rent rolls matter.
  • Houses of this age often have original wiring, plumbing and windows that a lender or inspector will question.
  • A cash offer already reflects the age of the building, so you do not have to renovate before closing.

Snow, roofs and repairs

A typical Worcester winter brings around 64 inches of snow, and total precipitation runs near 48 inches a year. The city stands higher than the ground around it and catches nor'easters, which is hard on roofs, gutters and pipes.

On a conventional listing, a buyer's inspector will go straight to the roof, the gutters and any ceiling stains. A sloped lot or one near a pond or brook deserves a note about drainage and any past water. Selling as is removes the repair back-and-forth, which suits an owner who would rather not spend money before the sale.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Worcester house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How Worcester bills property tax

Four bills arrive each year, and each falls due 30 days after the date it was issued. The fiscal year runs July 1 through June 30.

BillIssue dateType of bill
First quarterJuly 1Preliminary
Second quarterOctober 1Preliminary
Third quarterJanuary 1Actual
Fourth quarterApril 1Actual

Each preliminary bill is a quarter of last year's tax. The actual bills recalculate the year from the new assessment and rate, deduct the first two payments, and divide what is left between the final two. A value change from reassessment reaches you only on those last two bills.

Residential and commercial property carry different rates, posted as $13.28 and $29.06 per $1,000 of assessed value. No fiscal year is attached to those figures, so call Assessing for the rate in force now. Statewide rules are in our Massachusetts property tax guide.

Assessing office and abatements

Assessing works from City Hall, Room 209, 455 Main Street, and answers at 508-799-1098 or assessing@worcesterma.gov. The counter is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. until 5 p.m. Keep the property address and your newest bill within reach when you contact them.

  • An abatement application disputes your value or fixes a billing error, and it can be filed online.
  • Elderly, surviving spouse, blind and disabled veteran exemptions must be renewed by application each year.
  • Apartment and mixed-use owners are asked for yearly expense forms, which stay private.

Ask the office for the current abatement deadline before you plan around it.

State rules that come up at closing

Massachusetts law governs a Worcester sale, and three items nearly always show up.

  • Smoke detectors. Under M.G.L. c. 148, section 26F, the seller must install approved smoke detectors in a residential building when it is sold or transferred. The fire chief's office enforces this.
  • Deed excise. M.G.L. c. 64D, section 1 charges $2 for each $500 of consideration or fraction of it. Your closing attorney will figure the dollar amount.
  • Tax status. Request the balance on every bill from the city before closing so the attorney can pay them out of your proceeds.

Schedule the detector check early. It is a small job, but a missed one can hold up the closing date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Worcester houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a triple-decker with tenants

Renters living in the house do not rule out a cash sale. Talk to an attorney early about notices and security deposits, since occupied properties follow their own rules and we do not give legal advice. When you ask us for an offer, give the number of units, the rent on each and whether the tenants expect to stay. That information drives how the building is valued.

Selling with taxes owed

A bill you have not paid will not stop a sale. At closing, the title company or attorney requests each balance from the city and pays it out of your proceeds, so nothing comes out of your pocket beforehand. Because the third and fourth quarter bills reflect the reassessed value, the last two payments of the year are the ones most likely to differ from what you expected.

Before you list or accept an offer, collect the bills you have received this fiscal year and note which quarters are paid. If something looks wrong, an abatement application is the proper way to challenge the value. Ask Assessing whether bills still need to be paid on time while an abatement is under review, and keep paying until they tell you otherwise.

What to have ready before you call

  • Your latest real estate tax bill and the parcel address.
  • A list of any repairs, especially roof, heating and water damage from winter.
  • For a multifamily house, the number of units, the rent on each and whether any tenants plan to leave.
  • Any smoke detector paperwork you already hold.
  • The name of your closing attorney, if you already have one.

None of this has to be perfect. A rough picture of the house is enough for a first conversation, and we can fill in the rest together.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What a cash sale looks like in Worcester

No lender has to sign off on a cash purchase, and the house sells as is. We look at the address, condition, tax status and any tenants, and then send an offer. Accepting is your call.

  1. Tell us the address and describe the house in a few lines.
  2. We review it and respond with an offer.
  3. Once you say yes, a title company or attorney searches for liens and unpaid taxes.
  4. At closing the balances are paid from the proceeds and the rest goes to you.

People often choose this route after inheriting a house, moving away, or hitting repair costs they cannot cover before listing. You choose a closing date that works within reason. If you want to know what a Worcester offer could look like, reach out and we will answer plainly.

Frequently asked questions

How far is Worcester from Boston?

About 40 miles west of Boston and 38 miles northwest of Providence, Rhode Island. Interstates 90 and 290 and Route 146 link it to both.

When are Worcester property tax bills due?

Bills go out July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, and each is due 30 days later. The first two are preliminary and the last two are actual bills built on the new assessment.

How do I dispute my Worcester assessment?

File a real estate abatement application with the Assessing Division, online or on paper. Call 508-799-1098 for the form and the current deadline.

Do I need a smoke detector inspection to sell in Worcester?

Yes. The state requires approved smoke detectors in a residential building at sale or transfer, and the fire department head enforces the rule.

Can I sell a Worcester triple-decker with tenants?

Yes, a cash buyer can take a multifamily house with tenants in place. See an attorney about notices and deposits first, and give us the unit count and rents when you ask for an offer.

Where is Springfield, MA, and what is the city like?

Springfield is the largest city in Western Massachusetts and the seat of Hampden County, on the east bank of the Connecticut River. The 2020 census counted 155,929 residents, and the surrounding metro area is about 699,000.

The city covers 33.1 square miles, of which 31.9 are land. The Westfield River meets the Connecticut opposite the South End Bridge, and the Chicopee River joins just north of the city. The Connecticut state line is about four miles south, next to Longmeadow.

The Metro Center district around Main Street is flat and follows the river. Moving east, the ground turns hilly. Springfield has also been nicknamed "The City of Homes" and "A City in the Forest," and more than 4 square miles of it, about 12% of the land, is urban parkland.

A short history of Springfield

William Pynchon founded Springfield on May 14, 1636, and it became a city on May 25, 1852. The town was named for Springfield in Essex, England.

It was once much larger. Chicopee split off in 1852, Longmeadow in 1783 and West Springfield in 1774. The city also owns the Springfield Country Club, which sits inside West Springfield.

Springfield is known as "The City of Firsts," and in December 2022 the National Park Service designated it an American World War II Heritage City, the first in Massachusetts. Landmarks include the Basketball Hall of Fame, Symphony Hall and the Springfield Armory.

What are the neighborhoods of Springfield, MA?

Springfield is divided into 17 neighborhoods, and the housing in each can look very different. The list includes Bay, Boston Road, Brightwood, East Forest Park, East Springfield, Forest Park, Indian Orchard, Liberty Heights, McKnight, Memorial Square, Metro Center, Old Hill, Pine Point, Six Corners, Sixteen Acres, South End and Upper Hill.

  • Forest Park and Forest Park Heights surround a 735-acre park and include more than 600 Victorian "Painted Lady" houses
  • McKnight is described as the first planned residential neighborhood in the United States, with over 900 Painted Ladies
  • Indian Orchard grew as a mill town on the Chicopee River and still has a Main Street and former mill buildings
  • Liberty Heights holds Baystate Health, Mercy Medical and Shriners Children's hospital
  • Sixteen Acres, Pine Point and East Forest Park are mostly residential
  • East Springfield is residential and working-class, close to the former Smith & Wesson campus and a food distributor

Brightwood is cut off from the rest of the city by the elevated Interstate 91, a detail worth mentioning to buyers who care about noise or access.

Who are the big employers in Springfield?

Health care, insurance and manufacturing anchor the Springfield economy. A list drawn from the state labor agency names Baystate Medical Center, Smith & Wesson, General Dynamics, MassMutual, Mercy Medical Center, the U.S. Postal Service and Big Y Foods among the top city employers.

Smith & Wesson moved its corporate headquarters from East Springfield to Tennessee in 2023, though it planned to keep many Massachusetts jobs. MassMutual is a Fortune 100 company with its headquarters in the Pine Point area. In 2018, CRRC began assembling Orange Line cars in Springfield, and the city has also invested in a casino and a redeveloped Union Station.

The region markets itself as the Knowledge Corridor, with dozens of colleges within a short drive, including Springfield College, American International College and Springfield Technical Community College.

How does the weather affect a Springfield house?

Springfield has a hot-summer humid continental climate with cold winters. January averages about 26 degrees Fahrenheit, July about 74, and several days a summer top 90.

Annual snowfall averages 40.5 inches, mostly between mid-December and early March, and temperatures below zero can occur in any year. That makes the roof, insulation, heating system and gutters standard inspection topics.

On June 1, 2011, a tornado with winds above 160 miles per hour struck Springfield directly. It killed three people, left more than 500 homeless in the city and cut a 39-mile path from Westfield to Charlton. If your house was repaired after storm damage, keep the records, since buyers and their lenders may ask.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Springfield houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do roads and rail connect Springfield?

Springfield sits where north-south traffic along Interstate 91 meets east-west travel to Boston and New York. Union Station was redeveloped for roughly $95 million, and Peter Pan Bus Lines moved its Springfield terminal there in 2017.

The planned New Haven to Hartford to Springfield rail line was described as a $1 billion project. Anyone selling near Union Station or Metro Center may want to point out the walking distance to transit, while owners near the interstate should expect questions about traffic noise.

What steps apply when you sell a house in Massachusetts?

A Massachusetts home sale needs a fire department certificate showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale rules. The Department of Fire Services advises scheduling the inspection as soon as you have a closing date, and local departments charge a fee.

The alarm rules depend on the house's build date and the last building permit. Older battery smoke alarms must be swapped for ten-year sealed photoelectric units, and any alarm without a date stamp counts as expired.

The law library notes that most deeds are filed as recorded land at the county Registry of Deeds, and that attorneys are a regular part of closings. The same guide lists a state regulation on inspection waivers for certain residential sales, so ask your attorney whether it applies to your house.

What are your options to sell a house in Springfield?

Springfield owners can list, sell privately or accept a cash offer, and the right choice depends on the condition of the house and how soon you need to close.

  • Listing helps if the house is in showing condition and you can wait for a financed buyer
  • A private sale saves agent fees but puts the paperwork on you
  • A cash offer as-is suits inherited, damaged, vacant or tenant-occupied houses

Houses in the neighborhoods above vary a great deal, so a buyer or cash investor will price each address on its own condition, lot and block. Photos, a repair list and any utility or tax paperwork help any buyer decide quickly.

Older Victorian houses in Forest Park or McKnight may carry deferred maintenance that a financed buyer's lender will flag. A cash buyer can purchase without repairs, but the offer will reflect those needs.

Frequently asked questions

Springfield is in Hampden County in Western Massachusetts, on the east bank of the Connecticut River.

How many people live in Springfield, MA?

The 2020 census counted 155,929 people, which makes it the largest city in Western Massachusetts.

Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell in Springfield?

Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department when you sell. Call as soon as you set a closing date, and expect an inspection fee.

Can I sell a storm-damaged or older house in Springfield?

Yes. Buyers, including cash buyers, purchase houses with deferred repairs. Gather any repair records, since the price will reflect the condition.

Does Springfield get tornadoes?

They are rare, but a tornado struck Springfield directly on June 1, 2011, and caused significant damage across a 39-mile path.

Do I need an attorney to sell in Massachusetts?

Attorneys are a regular part of Massachusetts closings, by law and practice, according to the state court law library. Ask an attorney about your own sale.

Cambridge at a glance

Cambridge is a Middlesex County city facing Boston across the Charles River. The 2020 census counted 118,403 residents, and its ZIP codes run from 02138 to 02142. Land area is 6.4 square miles, so houses, triple-deckers and condos sit close together.

The city calls itself a city of squares. Most commercial districts form at big street intersections that double as neighborhood centers, which is how locals say where a house is.

Squares and neighborhoods buyers ask about

Buyers usually want to know which square a house is nearest.

  • Kendall Square, at Broadway, Main Street and Third Street, is the biotech and technology center beside MIT and the Kendall/MIT Red Line station.
  • Central Square, at Massachusetts Avenue, Prospect Street and Western Avenue, has a Red Line stop.
  • Harvard Square, at Massachusetts Avenue, Brattle Street and JFK Street, has the Harvard Red Line station and Cambridge Common nearby.
  • Porter Square has a Red Line stop and a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop.
  • Inman Square sits at Cambridge and Hampshire Streets, and Lechmere Square is next to CambridgeSide.

Cambridgeport, Baldwin and Mid-Cambridge fill out the map, and each has its own mix of houses. Naming the nearest square in your listing gives a buyer an instant picture of the location.

Getting around

The MBTA Red Line is the spine of the city, with stops at Kendall/MIT, Central, Harvard and Porter. Harvard Square is also a major bus terminal. If your house is a short walk from a Red Line stop, put it in the description, because it often matters more to a buyer than square footage.

How Cambridge values your property

The Assessing Department values property at full and fair cash value, which Massachusetts defines as 100 percent of fair market value. Appraisers weigh cost, income and market approaches, and the state Department of Revenue certifies the values before bills go out.

The city says owner-occupants can lower their bill through the residential exemption, and the FY27 application is due April 1, 2027. The Assessing page carries the current schedule, including the yearly abatement window.

Municipal lien certificates and water liens

A municipal lien certificate shows what is owed on a property, and a closing attorney will want one. Order it through the Finance Department at 617-349-4220.

Cambridge runs its own water system. A first-half FY27 tax bill can carry a Water and Sewer Lien, so read your bill closely. If one appears, phone the Finance Department before you list or sign a contract, so the balance does not surface at the closing table.

Why Cambridge sales get slow

Cambridge houses often come with complications: older construction, multi-unit buildings, tenants and historic districts.

  • Tenants in a two- or three-family can affect showings and the closing date.
  • Estate sales take time because of probate.
  • Condominium sales require documents from the association.
  • Older houses may need work before a buyer's lender will move forward.

None of these are city rules. They are common snags, and most of them add weeks. If one describes your situation, a direct cash sale avoids the showings and repairs.

The deed excise tax is $2.00 for each $500 of price or fraction of $500 under MGL c. 64D, s. 1, and the registry of deeds takes it when the deed is recorded. The department charges a fee, so book the visit once you have a closing date. Alarms that are ten years old or past expiration have to be swapped for ten-year sealed photoelectric models with a hush feature.

A sale here follows a familiar order. You accept an offer, sign a purchase agreement, clear any lien certificate items, pass the fire department inspection, and then sign the deed at closing. Condo owners add one more task: request the association's documents early, since waiting on them is a common cause of delay.

Without showings, a lender's appraisal or repair negotiations, you set the pace, and the closing date can follow your schedule, whether that means a lab contract starting soon or an estate that needs to wrap up.

Preparing the house and the paperwork

Start with the paper. A tidy folder saves days later. Pull the deed, the latest tax bill, any lien information and permit records for work you have done, especially kitchens, baths, additions and any finished attic or basement space. Buyers and their attorneys ask about permits on older Cambridge buildings, and a missing record can stall a closing.

For the house itself, an honest look at the roof, heating system, windows and wiring tells you whether a buyer's inspector will find surprises. Cosmetic work matters less than the big systems. If you cannot afford or do not want to do repairs, selling as is shifts that question to the buyer's price.

Selling an inherited or tenant-occupied house

Probate controls the timeline on an estate sale, and the personal representative usually cannot sign a deed until the court gives the go-ahead. Talk to an attorney about what is required first, then gather the death certificate paperwork, the deed and the tax bills.

With tenants, read each lease for its end date and notice terms. Showings need advance notice, and a buyer who plans to live in the unit may want it empty at closing. A cash buyer can often work around occupied units, which is why many Cambridge landlords and heirs ask about it.

Condo and multi-unit notes

Condominium sellers should ask the association for the master deed, the budget, the rules and any statement of unpaid fees well before listing. Multi-unit owners should tally rents, leases and any shared-system repairs. Organized files, handed over early and in one place, make a buyer more comfortable and shorten the time between agreement and closing, which matters whether the buyer is paying cash or relying on a lender.

When a cash sale fits

Some owners simply want a clean exit: a landlord tired of vacancies, heirs sharing an inherited two-family, or a household moving for a new job. In each case the question is whether time or a listing's potential extra price matters more. Ask each side to put terms in writing. Compare a written cash offer against an agent's estimate, subtract the repair costs and carrying costs, and choose the one that fits your calendar.

The 2020 census counted 118,403 people, fourth in the state behind Boston, Worcester and Springfield.

Applications for fiscal year 2027, residential or personal, are due April 1, 2027.

How do I contact the Cambridge Assessing Department?

Call 617-349-4343 or stop by 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor. Lien certificates go through the Finance Department at 617-349-4220.

Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell in Cambridge?

Yes. A compliance certificate from the local fire department is required by the state whenever a home is sold or transferred.

The Merrimack and Concord rivers meet in Lowell, a Middlesex County city that shares the traditional county seat title with Cambridge. The 2020 census counted 115,554 residents, the fifth most populous city in the state. The city covers 14.5 square miles, and it runs on a city manager and city council form of government.

Lowell was settled in 1652, became a town in 1826 and a city in 1836. The old mill district is now Lowell National Historical Park, and mill-era housing nearby makes up many of the homes sellers own.

Neighborhoods

Eight neighborhoods divide the city, and buyers form expectations from the one your house is in.

  • The Highlands (01851): the most populated area, with almost a quarter of residents. It lies in the southwest and includes Tyler Park, Drum Hill and the UMass Lowell South Campus.

Roads include Interstate 495, U.S. Route 3, the Lowell Connector and Massachusetts Routes 3A, 38, 110, 113 and 133. Local buses are run by the Lowell Regional Transit Authority, and the MBTA Lowell Line makes several daily trips to North Station. After a due date goes by, interest accrues at 14 percent a year. A $30 demand fee and demand notice follow after May 1, and unpaid real estate tax can become a lien. Escrow with a mortgage company does not remove your duty to confirm the bill was paid.

Write down the unit count and the target closing date so a buyer can answer quickly. Mill-era buildings often have separate meters, so note which utilities are shared among units, and keep the boiler service records where you can find them. Add a note on any repairs you have already made, such as a new roof or replaced windows, with the year and who did the work, since buyers value a paper trail. These small details tend to decide whether an offer arrives the same week or after a round of follow-up questions.

Late real estate tax accrues interest at 14 percent a year. After the May 1 due date, a $30 demand fee is added, and a demand notice is mailed for any unpaid bill.

No. A payment counts when the Treasurer's office receives it, so mail early or pay online. Rejected online payments can take up to three business days to become available again.

Middlesex County holds Lowell, so deeds are recorded in its Registry of Deeds, and copies can be searched at masslandrecords.com.

Villages and wards

Brockton is described through its villages and wards more than one downtown. Montello and Campello are villages with their own commuter rail stations and post offices. How the four tax bills work

Brockton issues four bills a year. The first two, on July 1 and October 1, are preliminary and based on last year's taxes. The third, issued January 1, is the actual bill with the new rate. The fourth is issued April 1. Each bill is due within 30 days of its issue date.

Four bills a year means a missed one stacks up quickly. Before talking price with anyone, check where your account stands.

How to appeal your assessment

To contest your valuation, the Board of Assessors needs your abatement application in hand, or postmarked, on or before February 1. A weekend February 1 pushes the cutoff to the following business day. Exemptions and deferrals have a separate clock: 90 days from the actual bill.

The office is at City Hall, 45 School Street, and the phone is 508-580-7194. Bring your bill and any evidence of value, such as repair estimates for a house in poor shape. Forms and details are on the city's assessors page.

The assessors also review deed recordings from the Plymouth County Registry of Deeds and building permits, then update the property's value. After you sell, expect the record to change.

In a normal Brockton year the sky drops roughly 50 inches of precipitation, about 34 of it snow, and the wind rarely quits. Snow, ice and the freeze and thaw cycle test older roofs, chimneys, gutters and foundation walls.

Mark the dates on a calendar: abatement applications by February 1, and exemptions and deferrals within 90 days of the actual bill. Missing either window means waiting a full year.

How a typical sale moves along

A traditional listing in Brockton usually goes in steps: you pick an agent, prepare the house, hold showings, negotiate with a buyer, wait for the buyer's inspection and financing, then close. Repairs a buyer's inspector flags can reopen the price talks, which is where an older house with an aging roof or chimney tends to slow down.

Whoever makes an offer, ask who pays the closing costs, how long the offer stays open, whether it depends on a financing approval or an inspection, and what date they can close. For a two- or three-family with tenants, find out whether the buyer plans to keep the leases. Tenants who stay put can make a sale simpler, and the rent roll you gathered becomes part of the sale file.

Why some Brockton owners choose a cash sale

Time pressure, a rough interior or tangled paperwork can make a regular listing a poor fit. Typical triggers: an inherited house, tenants in place, repairs put off for years, a job move on a tight clock, or back taxes.

With a cash buyer the house is judged in its present state. No open houses, no repair list, no waiting on a lender. Cash Home Buyers will walk through a Brockton house, then put a written number in front of you. Set it beside what a listing would cost in fees and months.

If you owe taxes, ask the collector's office what the balance is and raise it with your closing attorney before you set a price.

Is a cash sale right for you?

If the house shows well and you are in no rush, a listing may net more. We are not the right fit for every seller, and a cash offer is a choice you can compare with an agent's estimate. Get every offer on paper and read the line items.

Talk to your closing attorney, the fire department and the assessors early. The sooner you know the fire inspection date, the tax balance and the abatement deadline, the fewer surprises you will have between accepting an offer and handing over the keys.

Brockton is known as the City of Champions because boxers Rocky Marciano and Marvin Hagler came from there. It was also a leading shoe manufacturing city.

Thirty days after each issue date. Bills go out July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1.

February 1, by delivery or postmark, with the Assessor's Office. When that date lands on a weekend you get the next business day.

Lynn at a glance

Why Lynn houses are old

Europeans settled Lynn in 1629, and the city made shoes until the last factory closed in 1981. Electrical manufacturing followed, and Thomson-Houston Electric merged with Edison Electric in 1892 to form General Electric. The jet engine plant has stayed ever since.

Fire reshaped downtown twice. An 1889 blaze destroyed 296 buildings, including 142 homes, and in 1981 a fire at former shoe factories on Broad and Washington Streets burned 17 downtown buildings. Estates and beach cottages lined the shoreline in the mid-1800s, and Lynn Shore Drive opened in 1910 and drew more building along the coast. Many of those structures sit in the National Register Diamond Historic District.

Having these together lets a buyer give you a firm number sooner and keeps your attorney from chasing missing pages near the closing date.

Quincy at a glance

Norfolk County's largest city, Quincy, sits on Boston Harbor just south of the Neponset River. Boston lies to the north, Milton to the west, Randolph and Braintree to the south, and Weymouth and Hull across the water to the east. In 2020 the census found 101,636 residents, 46,789 households and 51,156 housing units.

The city covers 26.9 square miles, and about 37.6 percent of that is water. A big piece of the land is off the housing market entirely: the Blue Hills Reservation, a state park, takes up roughly 23 percent of the land area in the southwest corner and holds the city's high point, 517-foot Chickatawbut Hill. A house here is either on the harbor side, where Quincy Bay and Wollaston Beach shape daily life, or inland on the hills around Quincy Center, South Quincy and West Quincy.

Neighborhoods buyers think in

Buyers search by neighborhood in Quincy, so name yours in any description.

  • Wollaston: an early rail commuter area for Boston workers, now dense and mixed residential and commercial.
  • North Quincy: runs along Hancock Street and Quincy Shore Drive.
  • Quincy Center: the historic commercial and government core, with City Hall and the Thomas Crane Public Library.
  • Quincy Point: densely settled, east of the center, and the site of the Fore River Shipyard.
  • Houghs Neck and Squantum: peninsulas that began as summer resort areas and are now year-round neighborhoods.
  • Marina Bay: built in the 1980s on the former Naval Air Station Squantum, with high-rise condominiums and a large marina.
  • West Quincy: close to Interstate 93, with the old granite quarries.
  • Merrymount, Montclair, Adams Shore, Germantown and South Quincy: mostly residential.

A condo at Marina Bay and a single-family house on Houghs Neck draw different buyers, so pricing and marketing can differ a lot inside one city. The MBTA Red Line has four Quincy stops: North Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center and Quincy Adams. Interstate 93 and U.S. 1 run together through the west side, and Routes 3A, 28 and 53 cross the city.

Older houses and weather

Quincy grew in stages. Granite quarrying dominated 19th century jobs, and the Old Colony Railroad opened in 1845. The population grew by more than 50 percent in the 1920s, and shipbuilding at the Fore River Shipyard carried the 20th century. A single street can hold houses from several eras, and wiring, heating, roofs and smoke alarms can differ sharply from one to the next.

The winters are full New England ones. Average snowfall is 69.7 inches a year across about 29 snowy days, and January lows average 18.3 degrees Fahrenheit. Precipitation totals 53.86 inches a year over about 140 days. Buyers and inspectors look first at roofs, gutters, basements and heating systems, and at anything near Quincy Bay. If your house is close to the shore, ask your insurance agent and the city building department about flood mapping before you list.

State rules govern every sale in Quincy, and the deed goes on record in Norfolk County.

How Quincy bills property tax

Real estate tax in Quincy comes in four quarterly bills. Bills one and two are preliminary, together about 50 percent of last year's tax, due August 1 and November 1. Bills three and four apply the new assessed value and the current rate, less what you already paid, and fall due February 1 and May 1.

Property record cards are posted online, and a new valuation appears on the third-quarter bill each January. The assessors are at 1305 Hancock Street, phone (617) 376-1170. See the Quincy Assessors page for bill explanations.

Appealing your assessment

An overvalued house can be challenged by filing an abatement application. It must reach the assessors by the date the first installment is due, which in a quarterly city is generally February 1. Three months is how long the assessors have to answer. After their decision, three more months remain to take the case to the Appellate Tax Board. Late payments put the appeal at risk, so stay current while it moves.

If a sale is coming up this year, ask your closing attorney how the current quarter will be split at the table. Gather recent sales of comparable nearby houses and photographs before you file, since the owner carries the burden of showing the value is too high. A short, specific case does better than a general complaint, and the property record card posted online is a good place to check the facts the city holds on your house.

Paperwork to collect first

Most delays come from documents, not from the house. Before you speak with a buyer or an attorney, put these in one place: your deed, the latest tax bill, any permit records, a list of repairs you know the house needs and the contact details for the Quincy fire department.

If a mortgage is still open, ask your lender for a payoff figure. If you are selling an inherited house, talk to a probate attorney about court authority first. Then compare the routes side by side: a standard listing with repairs and showings, or a cash offer with a closing date you pick. Cash Home Buyers can buy a Quincy house in its present condition, and you can say no to any offer. Either way, the recording step at the Norfolk registry stays the same.

What Quincy sellers run into

Sellers in Quincy tend to land in one of four situations, each with a sensible first move.

  • A house that needs work: get a rough repair list before choosing between listing and a cash sale, so you compare real net numbers.
  • Alarm and certificate timing: book the fire department early so a missed inspection does not delay closing.
  • An inherited house: the estate may need court authority before it can sell, so talk to a probate attorney first.
  • Tight timelines: a job move or a payment problem favors a quick, certain closing over a long marketing period.

Every route, from a standard listing to a cash offer, ends at the same Norfolk County recording step. What differs is how many repairs, showings and weeks you need before you get there.

Yes. Quincy deeds are recorded at the Norfolk Registry of Deeds.

Yes. The fire department has to certify that the alarms meet state standards before a sale or transfer, so book the visit once a closing date is set.

What is the deed excise rate in Quincy?

The Norfolk registry collects $2.28 for each $500 of the price stated on the deed. Your attorney will work out the exact amount for your sale.

When are Quincy property taxes due?

Four times a year: August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.

With back taxes, request a payoff figure ahead of closing. The balance must be cleared so the buyer receives clear title. The climate is humid and moderated by the water, with about 52 inches of precipitation and 32.5 inches of snow a year. Rain or snow falls on roughly 124 days, and the January mean daily low is 22.1 degrees Fahrenheit.

Damp air, freeze and thaw cycles and salt exposure near the harbor wear on roofs, siding, basements and wood framing. Expect buyers to ask about gutters, foundations and older windows. Low ground, high ground and the harbor

The harbor is shared with Fairhaven, and the Roland J. Herbert Bridge links the two cities across Fish Island and Pope's Island. Clark's Point is the southernmost point of the city. That range matters when you describe a house. A home near the harbor faces different insurance and moisture questions than one on the hill, so know where your lot sits before you talk to a buyer or an insurer.

Interstate 195 is the main east-west route. It enters the city over the Charles M. Braga Jr. Memorial Bridge and runs through the middle of the city to Westport. The highway reaches New Bedford and Cape Cod to the east and Providence to the west, so Fall River works for commuters into Rhode Island, and that widens your buyer pool.

Water, hills and flood zones

Fall River has a long shoreline, a river and large ponds. The North Watuppa Pond is the main reservoir, and the Quequechan River drops steeply in its last half mile. Before listing, learn your parcel's flood zone from the city or an insurance agent. Lenders and buyers will request it.

If your basement has taken on water, tell buyers plainly and keep any repair receipts. Hillside lots raise a separate question about drainage and retaining walls, which an inspector will look at.

A century-old frame building on a slope gets close attention from inspectors. Knowing the answers to these in advance helps you set a realistic price.

Expect a buyer to ask how old the roof is, when the heating was last serviced, whether any unit has had water damage, and what the rents are. Answer from records where you can. Straight answers build trust and shorten the back-and-forth that slows a sale, whether the buyer is paying cash or relying on a bank.

Timeline from offer to closing

Newton's character is residential and varied. Some villages grew around old mill sites on the Charles River, while others were built out as streetcar and commuter neighborhoods, so house ages and conditions run across a wide range even on neighboring streets.

Two city offices split the work. Assessing determines what your house is worth on paper and rules on abatements, exemptions and excise adjustments. Treasury and Collector sends the bills and takes payment.

FY2027 exemption applications are due on or before April 1, 2027. If you plan to hold the house through the winter before you sell, put that date on your calendar.

Reaching the assessing office

Visit Newton City Hall, 1000 Commonwealth Avenue in Newton Centre, and ask for Room 111. The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and you can phone 617-796-1160.

Exemption, deferral and work-off programs are available to eligible owners. The Newton assessing page hosts the assessor's database and the application forms. Look up your own parcel before you speak with a buyer, because the database shows what the city has on file for your house.

Hills, rivers and wet basements

Newton grew up around seven hills: Nonantum, Waban, Chestnut Hill, Bald Pate, Oak Hill, Institution Hill and Mount Ida. Because the ground rises and falls from one village to the next, drainage, basements and the way a house sits on its lot are not the same everywhere. The Charles River borders the north and west of the city, and Crystal Lake, a 33-acre natural lake, lies in Newton Centre.

About 53.6 inches of precipitation fall in a typical year, and winters are cold, which is hard on roofs, chimneys, gutters and foundations. Near the river or the lake, an inspector may press on moisture and drainage. On a slope, grading is the usual question. If you know your basement has taken on water, say so to your attorney before you sign a purchase agreement.

Getting around Newton

Newton has MBTA light rail, commuter rail and bus service, and the Mass Pike crosses the northern part of town. Route 128 touches the western edge.

  • The Green Line D branch, known as the Riverside branch, goes through the middle of the city and ends at Newton Lower Falls. Riders reach downtown Boston in 10 to 30 minutes.
  • The B branch stops across from Boston College on Commonwealth Avenue.
  • Commuter rail on the Worcester line serves the northern villages near Waltham.
  • Express buses use the Mass Pike to reach downtown Boston.
  • Routes 9, 30 and 16 run east to west. Nearly every north-south street ends inside the city, so Newton has no major north-south road.

The Newtonville commuter rail station is scheduled to close in December 2026 for accessibility work and reopen in spring 2029. A house close to that station may get questions from commuters.

What closing requires in Newton

A typical Newton sale involves a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate issued by the fire department, clear title and nearly always an attorney.

  • Set the alarm inspection as soon as a closing date exists. What the inspector checks depends on when the house was built and when its last permit was issued.
  • Replace any battery alarm that is expired or lacks a date with a sealed 10-year photoelectric model with a hush feature.
  • Your deed is recorded at the county registry of deeds. The Secretary of the Commonwealth runs an email alert that tells you when a new document is recorded against your property.
  • The deeds excise follows Chapter 64D, Section 1 and is figured per $500 of price.

Land Court registered land is rarer than recorded land in Massachusetts. Your attorney will tell you which type your lot is.

Paperwork to gather before you call

Preparation shortens the timeline. Pull together your deed, the latest tax bill, permit records for any work done on the house and any notes about water in the basement. For an estate, add the court or estate paperwork, because heirs have to show authority before a deed can pass to a buyer.

Ask the Assessing Department whether an exemption or deferral on your bill ends when the property changes hands. Your attorney will also need payoff figures for any mortgage or unpaid tax balance. When these documents sit in one folder, the attorney reviews them once instead of chasing pieces over several weeks.

A short sequence works for most owners. Start with the tax bill and the assessor record. Book the alarm inspection once a date is set. Hand everything to the attorney, then compare the offer with the dates and repairs a regular listing would involve. Nobody can make you take an offer, and you can ask for a different closing date.

Selling an older Newton house

Plenty of Newton owners hold a house that needs updating, or they are settling an estate or moving on short notice. A mortgage buyer's inspection can turn up alarm upgrades and repair items on an older house, and sellers often reach for a cash sale to avoid that round of negotiation.

A cash buyer removes lender approval from the schedule. The fire certificate, title work and recording happen regardless, and a tax balance has to be cleared before the deed goes over. Cash Home Buyers can look at a Newton house as it stands and you owe nothing if you decline. Set the offer next to what a listing would involve in repairs, showings and time, and pick the route that suits you. If a relocation or an estate sets the deadline, tell the buyer early so the closing date can be planned around it from the start.

Frequently asked questions

How many villages are in Newton, MA?

Newton has thirteen villages: Auburndale, Chestnut Hill, Newton Centre, Newton Corner, Newton Highlands, Newton Lower Falls, Newton Upper Falls, Newtonville, Nonantum, Oak Hill, Thompsonville, Waban and West Newton.

What is the Newton residential property tax rate?

The certified FY2026 residential rate is $9.69 per $1,000 of assessed value. Commercial, industrial and personal property is taxed at $18.06.

Does Newton have a Green Line stop?

Yes. The D branch crosses the middle of the city to Newton Lower Falls, and the B branch ends at Boston College on the Brighton line.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Newton?

Yes. Massachusetts requires one from the local fire department whenever a home is sold or transferred. The department charges a fee, so call to book the visit.

When is the Newton exemption application deadline?

Applications for FY2027 exemptions and tax assistance are due on or before April 1, 2027. Call the assessing office to confirm which forms apply to you.

Lawrence at a glance

Lawrence is a compact city in Essex County, straddling the Merrimack River about 30 miles north-northwest of Boston. Its 89,143 residents (2020 census) share just 7.4 square miles, which works out to roughly 12,864 people per square mile. Methuen lies to the north, North Andover to the east and Andover to the south and southwest. Lawrence is also one of Essex County's two county seats, alongside Salem, so the district and superior courts sit here.

Four ZIP codes cover the city: 01840, 01841, 01842 and 01843.

Mill-era housing

The Essex Company began the Great Stone Dam in 1845, Lawrence became a town in 1847, and it was chartered as a city in 1853. Canals fed the mills, and workers arrived from Ireland, Germany, Sweden and French Canada, then from Italy and Eastern Europe. The nickname Immigrant City stuck.

Housing grew up around those mills: historic rowhouses and mill-era buildings packed into a small footprint. Many properties are older and hold more than one unit, so a seller here is often handling a multi-unit building rather than a single house. Age, wiring and heating systems drive most buyer questions.

Areas and landmarks

Lawrence uses six council districts, and residents also place themselves by landmark.

  • Downtown and the canals: the North Canal, Great Stone Dam and mill buildings such as the Ayer Mills clock tower.
  • South Lawrence: the Shawsheen Fields area, where the first settlement in the present city began in 1655.
  • Tower Hill: high ground in the northwest, home to the 1895 High Service Water Tower.
  • Prospect Hill and Mount Vernon: hills on the northeastern and southern edges.
  • Den Rock Park: a wooded conservation area on the southern line shared with Andover.

When you describe a property to a buyer, name the area and the nearest landmark.

Getting around

Interstate 495 crosses the eastern part of the city with three exits inside the limits. Route 28 runs north to south, Route 110 crosses the northern half, and Route 114 ends at Route 28 by the river. Lawrence is the western hub for Merrimack Valley Regional Transit Authority buses and has a stop on the MBTA Haverhill Line to North Station.

With highway, bus and commuter rail in one small city, buyers who work elsewhere in the region may consider a Lawrence house. Mention nearby transit in your description.

Tax bills and phone numbers

Real estate bills go out quarterly, on the first business day of July, October, January and April. Payment is due the first business day of August, November, February and May. Rates change each year, and you can estimate a bill by multiplying assessed value by the rate per $1,000.

OfficePhoneCall about

The Treasurer/Collector's page on cityoflawrence.com also offers a tax bill lookup.

How to appeal your assessment

File an abatement application with the Assessor on the approved form. It has to reach the assessors by the due date of the first installment of the actual bill, usually February 1 where bills are quarterly. The assessors then have three months to answer before the application is treated as denied.

You also need to have paid every installment on time. Check the details on your own bill and phone the Assessor before the deadline. If you plan to sell within weeks, an appeal will probably not finish first, so weigh whether it is worth the effort.

Gas service and heating records

On September 13, 2018, a series of gas explosions and fires hit as many as 40 homes across Lawrence, Andover and North Andover. One resident died, and more than 30,000 customers left their homes. A second leak a year later, on September 27, 2019, again forced evacuations.

Some buyers still ask about a home's heating system, the gas service and its age. Keep records of any boiler, furnace or gas line work, and hand the paperwork over early. A cash buyer will usually inspect the system in person anyway.

What a sale involves

An attorney handles title and closing work. Massachusetts keeps two title systems: recorded land, filed with the Registry of Deeds, and registered land, filed through the Land Court.

Two state items catch many sellers off guard.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. The fire department inspects alarms and issues a certificate of compliance. Book it as soon as a closing date is set.
  • Home inspection waivers. State rule 760 CMR 74 limits sellers of certain residential properties from conditioning offers on a buyer's waiver of inspection.

Deed excise is $2 per $500 of consideration and is usually paid by the seller. Ask the Essex County registry for the current total before you sign.

Selling a multi-family or inherited property

Older and multi-unit housing creates a few situations that come up again and again.

  • An inherited two- or three-family house with tenants and no one to manage it.
  • Roof, porch or heating repairs that cost more than the owner can fund.
  • Unpaid taxes or water charges that need a payoff.
  • A house on a small lot, which can narrow the pool of conventional buyers.

If you ask for a cash offer, we look at the building as it is and tell you what we would pay. Set that number against repair costs and the time a listing would take.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What a cash sale skips

A cash buyer does not need a lender, so there is no appraisal ordered by a bank, no loan commitment to wait on and no financing contingency that can collapse a week before closing. Showings are limited to a visit or two, and you are not asked to repaint, patch a roof or clear out every room first.

Everything required by Massachusetts still applies. The alarm certificate, title search, payoff letters and deed recording all happen, and your attorney still reviews the purchase and sale agreement. What changes is the number of parties who can delay you.

What to line up before closing

Collect the current tax bill, any water balance, mortgage payoff statements and tenant lease copies if units are rented. Ask the Collector whether anything is overdue, because unpaid balances get settled from your proceeds. Book the fire department visit early, since a failed alarm check is a fixable delay only if you leave time to fix it.

If the house came through an estate, the attorney will also want the papers showing who may sign the deed. Having all of this in one folder shortens the path from accepted offer to funds in your account, and it lets a buyer's attorney answer title questions without sending you back to the office for another copy.

Frequently asked questions

When are Lawrence property tax bills due?

Real estate bills are due on the first business day of August, November, February and May. They are issued on the first business day of July, October, January and April.

Who do I call about my Lawrence assessed value?

Call the Lawrence Assessor at (978) 620-3190. For overdue balances or tax title accounts, the Collector's office takes calls at (978) 620-3170.

Is a smoke detector inspection required to sell in Lawrence?

Yes. Massachusetts requires a fire department certificate of compliance when a home is sold or transferred. Contact the department to schedule the visit and ask about the fee.

What county is Lawrence in?

Lawrence is in Essex County, Massachusetts, one of two county seats along with Salem. Deeds for Lawrence properties are recorded through the Essex County registry system.

Can I sell a Lawrence multi-family house as-is?

Yes. You can sell the building in its current condition. Expect the buyer to review the units, tenants and systems, and plan for the fire department certificate and any tax payoff.

Where is Somerville, MA, and how big is it?

Somerville is a city directly northwest of Boston and north of Cambridge, in Middlesex County. It covers about 4.2 square miles, of which roughly 4.1 is land, and the 2020 census counted 81,045 residents.

That makes Somerville the most densely populated municipality in New England. Its neighbors are Cambridge, Medford, Everett, Arlington and the Charlestown section of Boston, and it sits on the west bank of the Mystic River. ZIP codes run from 02143 to 02145.

For a seller, the density shows up in the housing itself. Lots are small, houses sit close together, and a neighbor's fence line, driveway or shared wall often becomes part of the conversation with any buyer.

A short history of Somerville

English settlers first used the land in 1629 as part of Charlestown, and Somerville became its own town in 1842 and a city in 1872. For more than two centuries it was farmland and cow pasture, which is why early maps call it "beyond the Neck."

The Old Powder House on Broadway, where the colonial government kept the largest supply of gunpowder in Massachusetts, was emptied by British troops on September 1, 1774. Historians treat that raid as a rehearsal for Lexington and Concord. Railroads and slaughterhouses later filled in the Millers River marsh, and the city industrialized in the mid-1800s.

The city received the All-America City Award in 1972, 2009 and 2015. Whatever the age of your house, buyers will ask about wiring, heating and any past additions.

What are the Seven Hills and squares of Somerville?

Somerville is built on seven glacial ridges, and its commercial life gathers in squares instead of one downtown. The hills are Central, Clarendon, Cobble, Ploughed (Mount Benedict), Prospect, Spring and Winter Hill.

The squares and neighborhoods listed for the city include:

  • Davis Square, known for theaters, music venues and restaurants
  • Union Square, one of the oldest settled areas
  • Assembly Square, with large-format retail and highway access
  • Ball, Magoun, Gilman and Powder House Squares
  • East Somerville, Winter Hill, Ten Hills and Brickbottom

The hills decide where roads and shops could go, according to the city history. If you sell on a slope, say so plainly, and note how far the nearest square or station is.

Mass General Brigham moved its headquarters to Assembly Square in 2016, and other offices have since opened in Assembly Row and Union Square. Companies based in the city also include Gentle Giant Moving Company and Candlewick Press.

Transit is one of the biggest value points for a Somerville property. The Red Line Northwest Extension reached Davis Square in 1984, and the Green Line Extension opened in 2022 with five new stations inside the city.

Old routes still shape the grid. Washington Street dates to the 1630s as the road to Cambridge, Broadway carried trolleys from 1858, and Somerville Avenue was once "Milk Row" for dairy farmers heading to market.

The Green Line Extension has put pressure on affordability for some residents. If your house sits near a new station, buyers will already know that, so you do not need to oversell it.

Tufts University has a campus on the Somerville and Medford line, with the municipal border running through its Tisch Library. If your house has tenants, mention the lease terms early, because buyers will ask.

Every seller of a home in Massachusetts needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale rules. The Department of Fire Services says to call the department as soon as you have a closing date, and the department charges a fee for the inspection and certificate.

Alarm requirements depend on the year the house was built and the date of the last building permit. Battery-powered smoke alarms older than ten years must be replaced with photoelectric units that have sealed ten-year batteries and a hush feature. Alarms with no manufacture date are treated as expired.

The state law library also points out that attorneys are a regular part of Massachusetts closings, by law and practice, and that most deeds are recorded land filed at the county Registry of Deeds. You can search your own deed and mortgage records on masslandrecords.com. Ask the Somerville Inspectional Services Division and the fire department about local steps, since city rules vary and change.

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or take a cash offer, and each path trades time against effort. Listing may reach the widest buyer pool but means repairs, showings and a financing contingency.

  • Cash offer as-is: a faster, simpler close with a buyer who does not need a mortgage

Cash buyers tend to fit situations like inherited houses, tenant-occupied buildings, deferred repairs and looming bills. Compare any offer to what you would net after agent fees, repairs and carrying costs.

Framingham in brief

Framingham is a Middlesex County city in the MetroWest part of Greater Boston, about 25 square miles of land with 72,362 residents at the 2020 census. It was a town for more than 300 years, and voters approved a mayor and council charter in April 2017. The city form began on January 1, 2018.

After World War II the town grew quickly, and much of the housing from that period is split-level and ranch style. Sellers of those homes often deal with original kitchens, older baths and systems that have never been updated.

Areas sellers hear about most

Framingham is split into business districts and villages, and a house in each tends to attract a different buyer.

  • Golden Triangle: the retail and office district on the east side, bordered by Route 9, Route 30 and Speen Street. TJX has its world headquarters at Route 30 and Speen Street.
  • Downtown and South Framingham: the commercial center that grew with the railroad in the 1880s.
  • West Framingham: centered on Route 9 with large office parks and most of the city's apartment and condominium complexes.
  • Framingham Centre, Saxonville and Nobscot: older villages. The Framingham Centre Common Historic District is the historic center, with Framingham State University beside it.

A house near Route 9 can draw steady rental interest and also carry heavy traffic noise. Renters, commuters and office-park employees all show up as potential occupants.

Transit and highway access

Framingham sits roughly halfway between Boston and Worcester. The Massachusetts Turnpike (Interstate 90), Route 9, Route 30, Route 126 and Route 135 all cross the city.

Downtown is split by the rail tracks and Waverly Street (Route 135). Homes within walking range of the station draw commuters, while houses near the Turnpike and Route 9 interchanges draw buyers who want quick highway access.

Schools buyers ask about

Buyers with children usually ask which elementary school serves a house. Get the school assignment from the district before you list or negotiate, and have the answer ready. A wrong guess costs trust, so confirm it rather than assume. Families often decide on the school before they look at the kitchen.

Property tax installments

Framingham bills property tax quarterly, with installments due on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Payments after the due date accrue interest at 14 percent per year under G.L. c. 59, s. 57C, counted from the day after the due date.

The city tries to mail bills at least 30 days before each due date. Not receiving a bill does not remove the obligation, so contact the Tax Collector if nothing arrives two or three weeks before a date. The Treasurer/Collector is at 150 Concord Street, Room 111, phone 508-532-5430.

If you sell in the middle of a billing quarter, the closing statement normally adjusts the current installment between seller and buyer. Ask your closing attorney which installments are paid and which are still open. The city explains more on its Important Tax Information page.

Smoke and carbon monoxide inspection

Selling a one or two family home requires a Fire Department smoke and carbon monoxide detector inspection before closing. Apply and pay online, then call Fire Department Administration at 508-532-5930 to schedule the visit.

  • Allow at least three weeks between the inspection request and your closing date.
  • Inspections are generally held Monday to Friday, typically in the afternoon.
  • The house number must be on the structure itself, not on a door, at least 3 inches tall and visible from the nearest street.
  • Fire Headquarters is at 10 Loring Drive.

A failed inspection is a common reason a closing slips by a few days. Replacing old alarms before you apply is usually cheaper than a second visit. The city's inspection page links the requirements sheet.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Framingham houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What Framingham sellers usually run into

  • Mid-century houses with dated systems that need work before a conventional buyer's lender will approve them.
  • Inherited homes where the owner lives out of state and has not cleared the contents.
  • Tenant-occupied homes and multi-family properties, especially near downtown and along Route 9.
  • Open tax installments, or a closing date that has to fit around the three-week fire inspection lead time.

A cash buyer who purchases as is can skip repair lists and showings, which matters most on inherited and tenant-occupied properties. You still need a clear title, an inspection certificate and tax adjustments at closing, so line those up early.

How do you decide between listing and a cash sale?

Listing makes sense when the house is in good shape and you can wait out showings, an appraisal and a buyer's financing. A cash sale makes sense when time, condition or occupancy is the bigger problem.

Compare net amounts, not headline prices. A listing involves agent commission, repairs a lender may require and weeks of carrying costs such as tax installments and utilities. A direct sale removes several of those lines, along with the uncertainty of a buyer's financing falling through, but usually comes at a lower number. Ask any buyer for the offer in writing, and ask the closing attorney what you would actually receive after the mortgage payoff and tax adjustments.

Preparing a mid-century house

Split-levels and ranches from the postwar years often still have the original kitchen, an older bath and a heating or electrical system that has never been replaced. A buyer's lender may want some of that fixed before it will approve a loan, which is where deals stall. You have three choices: repair before listing, offer a credit, or sell as is. Get a contractor's quote for the biggest item, usually the roof, the heating system or the panel, so you know what each choice costs. Put the quotes beside a written cash offer and a listing estimate, and the best path for your situation usually becomes clear.

Gather permit records for any additions or finished basements, since a missing permit is a question the buyer's attorney will ask.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

A sample timeline

Work backward from your closing date. At least three weeks out, file the fire inspection request. Before that, order any alarm replacements and put the house number on the structure. A few weeks earlier still, ask the Treasurer/Collector which installments are open, gather the deed and permit records, and talk to your closing attorney about the mortgage payoff. Doing these in order, with a date next to each, keeps a few days of slip from turning into a missed date.

Frequently asked questions

Is Framingham a town or a city?

A city. Voters approved a mayor and council charter in April 2017, and the city form took effect on January 1, 2018.

Do I need a smoke and carbon monoxide inspection to sell in Framingham?

Yes. The Fire Department inspects the detectors for sales, and the city asks for at least three weeks of lead time before your closing date.

When are Framingham property tax bills due?

Installments are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Late payments carry 14 percent annual interest.

Which train line serves Framingham?

The MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line runs to South Station and Back Bay. The trip to Back Bay takes about 42 to 45 minutes.

Can I sell a Framingham house that has tenants?

Yes, and some cash buyers purchase tenant-occupied homes as is. The lease stays in force, so ask the buyer how they handle the tenancy before you sign.

Haverhill at a glance

Haverhill sits on the Merrimack River in Essex County, hard against the New Hampshire line, roughly 35 miles up the road from Boston. The 2020 census counted 67,787 residents, and the 2024 estimate is 68,291. The population grew 11.3 percent between 2010 and 2020, and a growing town tends to keep buyers searching, though no price is promised.

Housing is mostly owner stock mixed with rentals: 26,696 households live in 27,927 housing units, and 4.4 percent of those units were vacant. The homeowner vacancy rate was 0.8 percent, so hardly any owned homes stood empty.

Neighborhoods buyers ask about

Buyers sort Haverhill houses by district first, so say which one yours is in. The Merrimack separates the Bradford section from the rest of the city.

  • Downtown: rezoned to encourage artist live-work lofts and educational uses, with a parking garage, boardwalk and boat docks along the river.
  • The Highlands: the district beside downtown, known for Victorian mansions built during the shoe boom.
  • Bradford: across the river, and home to the Bradford MBTA station.
  • Ward Hill and Rocks Village: Rocks Village is a historic district with early architecture, including the 1691 Kimball Tavern.

Winnekenni Park, a conservation area with Winnekenni Castle and Lake Saltonstall, is among the city's best known open spaces. Say so if you live near it.

Older homes and what buyers look at

Haverhill housing runs from colonial-era houses to Victorian mansions and converted mill lofts. Shoe manufacturing built the city, and Bradford joined it on January 1, 1897. Downtown rezoning has turned old factories into loft apartments and condominiums, with about $150 million in public and private investment in the old factory district.

A house that is a few generations old will get a close look at its roof, heating system and basement. Snow loads on roofs, ice dams in gutters and damp basements close to the river are what local inspectors flag most. Keep repair receipts and permit papers handy; they settle questions fast.

Getting around Haverhill

Interstate 495 runs through the city with five exits, and Routes 97, 108, 110, 113 and 125 cross it. Routes 108 and 125 end at the New Hampshire line and continue into that state.

  • MBTA Commuter Rail serves the Haverhill and Bradford stations on the Haverhill/Reading Line to North Station.
  • Amtrak also stops at the Haverhill station, with service to Portland, Maine and Boston.
  • MeVa Transit runs local buses in and beyond the city.
  • Logan International Airport in Boston is the nearest international airport.

Commuters ask first about distance to an I-495 exit or a rail station, so have that answer ready.

Tax due dates and late interest

The four yearly installments for real estate and personal property fall on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Anything unpaid on those dates collects 14 percent interest.

The early bills are estimates built from the previous fiscal year's actual net bill. The city's formula is last year's actual tax times 2.5 percent, added to the actual, then divided by four. Unpaid balances after May 1 can lead to a tax lien, and new liens after November 2024 carry 8 percent interest. Liens are recorded with the Registry of Deeds, which means a buyer's attorney will find it in the title search.

Back taxes are normally paid from your sale proceeds at closing. Get a payoff figure from the collector before you settle on a date.

Tax bills after you sell

If a sale happens after the January 1 assessment, the bill remains in the January 1 owner's name. The buyer has to call the Assessors at 978-374-2316 for a duplicate, and your attorney normally divides the year's tax between you in the closing adjustments.

Abatement applications must reach the Assessors on or before February 1. Think your value is too high? Watch that date if you plan to keep the house another year. A quick sale rarely leaves time for an appeal to matter. Current forms and payment options are on the tax payment page.

Before any residential sale closes, the Haverhill Fire Prevention Office checks the smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, under M.G.L. Chapter 148, Section 26F and 26F 1/2. Inspections are done on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and only a limited number can be done each day, so book early.

The city will not schedule the inspection until payment is received. You will get an email with the date and a call with the appointment time. Applications and details are on the fire department's page, or call 978-373-8460.

Timing the inspection with your closing

The certificate stays valid for 60 days. Schedule it near enough to closing that it will not expire, yet early enough to swap out a failed alarm. One workable order: sign the contract, request the inspection at once, pay the fee, and file the certificate with your closing papers.

Have the building's age, the unit count and any alarm receipts ready for the visit. If the inspector flags something, fix it and ask about a reinspection.

Papers to gather first

A thin folder speeds everything up: your latest tax bill, any lien notice, a mortgage payoff statement if you have a loan, and receipts for roof, boiler or electrical work. For an inherited house, add the papers showing who has authority to sign.

Then jot down the street address, the unit count, whether anyone rents a unit, and your target closing date. With those four details a buyer can quote a realistic price and schedule.
