From offer to closing in Haverhill

Once you accept an offer, an attorney reviews the contract and runs the title search. The search turns up mortgages, tax liens and anything else recorded against the house, and each one needs a payoff letter or a release. Meanwhile the fire inspection gets booked, and the deed is prepared for recording at the Registry of Deeds.

On closing day you sign the deed and the settlement statement, the buyer's funds are delivered, and the attorney pays off your lenders and any taxes from the proceeds. You get the remainder. With a cash buyer there is no loan approval in the middle, so the usual delays are title problems and a missed alarm inspection. Handle those two early and the rest tends to go quickly.

Cash sale or listing

Plenty of local sellers hold older houses that need updating, or inherited property they cannot easily manage. Selling as-is for cash suits a house that needs work. It skips the lender appraisal, financing contingencies and most showings, and closing can follow your calendar.

A house in good shape may net more on the open market. Compare what each route leaves you after repairs, carrying costs and waiting time, and have an attorney read any contract first.

Is Haverhill in Essex County?

Yes. Haverhill is the largest city or town in Essex County, located on the Merrimack River at the New Hampshire border.

When are Haverhill property tax payments due?

Installments fall on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, and late ones accrue 14 percent interest.

How long is a Haverhill smoke detector certificate valid?

Sixty days. Haverhill inspects on Tuesdays and Thursdays and does not schedule until payment is received.

What does a Haverhill smoke and CO inspection cost for one home?

The fee for one residential unit is $50. Two units cost $100, and larger buildings cost more.

Who gets the tax bill after I sell my Haverhill house?

The January 1 owner's name stays on the bill. The buyer asks the Assessors for a duplicate, and closing adjustments split the cost.

Squares and neighborhoods

Malden grew around squares at its crossroads, and many neighborhoods take the name of the square at their center.

Maplewood got its name in 1847, when the president of the Saugus Branch Railroad bought 200 acres and planned wide streets with ornamental maples. Edgeworth was once the site of the Converse Rubber Factory, the original home of the Converse sneaker.

Why the housing runs old

Puritans settled Malden in 1640, the town was incorporated in 1649, and it became a city in 1882. It once included Melrose, which separated in 1850, and Everett, which separated in 1870. The first mayor funded the Converse Memorial Library, built in 1885.

That long history means older housing. A house built a century or more ago can come with original layouts, older heating systems and decades of deferred work, and buyers who use a mortgage will see those items in their own inspection. A cash buyer prices them directly.

  • U.S. Route 1 is the one limited access route through the city, linking Boston and the North Shore.
  • Routes 28, 60 and 99 run through as arterial roads.
  • Route 16 and Interstate 93 are a short distance outside the city line.

The Northern Strand Trail, also called the Bike to the Sea trail, gives a paved route from the Mystic River in Everett to Western Avenue in Lynn. Houses within walking distance of a station draw commuters, which helps a listing, but a cash buyer prices a house on its condition and numbers either way.

The Massachusetts Department of Fire Services requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing that your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the standard for a sale or transfer.

Ask the City of Malden's building and assessing offices about permits and bills tied to your address, and ask your attorney who pays the excise under your contract.

Ask the buyer whether they will keep tenants or need the unit empty. Many Malden sellers own a two or three family house with a mix of long-term and short-term tenants, so gather lease copies, rent records and any security deposit details before you ask for offers.

How a cash sale works

Listing the same house means preparing it, showing it and waiting on a buyer's loan. Selling for cash trades a possible higher price for speed and certainty. For a Malden multifamily with tenants or an estate house full of belongings, that trade is worth thinking through.

At the table you sign the deed and the settlement statement, your lenders and any back taxes are paid from the proceeds, and you keep what is left.

With no bank involved, the usual causes of delay are an old lien nobody remembered and an alarm inspection booked too late. In an older two or three family with several floors, a hard-wired alarm that fails can mean calling an electrician, so book the visit early enough to fix it.

What to bring to the table

Where is Waltham, MA?

Waltham is a Middlesex County city on the Charles River, about 9 to 11 miles west of downtown Boston. The 2020 census counted 65,218 residents, and the 2024 estimate was 65,849.

It borders Watertown and Belmont to the east, Lexington to the north, Lincoln and Weston to the west, and Newton to the south. The city covers about 13.7 square miles, with around 12.7 square miles of land, and has ZIP codes 02451 to 02454.

The center of Waltham is the Common on Main Street, where City Hall, the public library and the post office stand. The river runs through town with several dams that once powered the mills.

Why is Waltham called the Watch City?

The Waltham Watch Company opened its factory here in 1854 and was the first to make watches on an assembly line. It produced over 35 million watches, clocks and instruments before it closed in 1957.

Waltham also hosted the Boston Manufacturing Company, whose model of mill and worker housing became known as the Waltham-Lowell system. The English settled the area in 1634 as part of Watertown, and Waltham became a separate town in 1738 and a city in 1884.

The city also holds large historic estates, including Gore Place (built in 1806), the Robert Treat Paine Estate and the 400-acre Lyman Estate.

How has Waltham's population changed?

Waltham grew quickly during the mill era, dipped after 1970, and has climbed again since 2000. Census figures show a peak of 61,582 in 1970, a fall to 57,878 by 1990 and a rise to 65,218 in 2020.

The 7.6 percent rise between 2010 and 2020 was the fastest since the 1960s. Population alone does not set a house price, so judge your own sale by the condition and location of the house.

Which neighborhoods make up Waltham?

Waltham is a patchwork of named villages, and each has its own character and housing mix. The list includes:

  • The Highlands, Piety Corner and Warrendale
  • The Bleachery, named for a former dye works, and The Chemistry, named for a former chemical company
  • Banks Square, Ellison Park, Cedarwood and Gardencrest
  • The Island, The Lanes, Ravenswood and Roberts
  • Kendal Green, mostly in Weston, and Wildwood Acres

Moody Street downtown has shops, restaurants and nightlife and is sometimes called Restaurant Row. Its access to the Commuter Rail and lower rents have drawn younger professionals in the twenty-first century. A seller near Moody Street can reasonably highlight that, while owners elsewhere may lean on quiet streets or the river trails.

Who are the largest employers in Waltham?

Waltham mixes universities, life sciences, utilities and corporate offices. The city's 2023 annual financial report lists the largest non-city employers as Bentley University, Brandeis University, Fresenius Medical Care, National Grid, Constant Contact and Vistaprint, each with 1,000 to 4,999 employees.

Others on the list include Eversource, MetLife and Sanofi Genzyme. Companies based in town include Revvity, RTX (headquarters of its Raytheon business), Thermo Fisher Scientific, Alkermes, Boston Dynamics and Pegasystems.

The city is also a base for regional offices. Wolverine World Wide moved its regional headquarters to the CityPoint campus in July 2016, and C & J Clark America moved to the former Polaroid site that October.

Retail concentrates on Main, Moody, Lexington and River Streets, parts of Route 60, the First Avenue area and a former Polaroid site that has seen new development. Because so many people work in town, owners with a job change, a divorce or an inherited house may need a quick answer on timing.

How do you get around Waltham?

Waltham is close to Interstate 95, which runs with Route 128 through the west of the city, and the Massachusetts Turnpike (I-90) is just south in Newton. Route 20 follows an old native trail called the Old Connecticut Path.

The MBTA Commuter Rail has two Waltham stops on the Fitchburg Line, one at Central Square across from City Hall and one near Brandeis. MBTA buses include routes 61, 70, 170, 505, 553, 554, 556 and 558. The Charles River path lets some residents bike to offices in Cambridge and Boston.

Distance to the train and to Route 128 sits near the top of most commuter buyers' lists, so list those distances when you sell. The city a walkability score of 62 out of 100 for central and south Waltham.

Which schools serve Waltham, MA?

Waltham Public Schools run seven elementary schools, two middle schools and one high school. The elementary schools are Northeast, Fitzgerald, MacArthur, Plympton, Whittemore, Stanley and the Waltham Dual Language Elementary School.

The middle schools are McDevitt and Kennedy, and Waltham High School teams are the Hawks. Higher education includes Bentley and Brandeis, and private schools include Chapel Hill-Chauncy Hall and Gann Academy. The Waltham Times, a nonprofit online news outlet started in 2024, covers city news.

A Waltham seller must obtain a certificate of compliance from the local fire department, showing the home's smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet state sale rules. The Waltham Fire Department has 166 full-time firefighters and a fire prevention division, so ask it how to schedule the inspection.

Where is Taunton, MA, and how large is it?

Taunton is the county seat of Bristol County in southeastern Massachusetts, on the Taunton River about 10 miles north of Mount Hope Bay. The city had 59,408 residents in the 2020 census, which places it third in Bristol County behind New Bedford and Fall River.

It covers 48.4 square miles, of which about 46.4 are land, making Taunton the third-largest city by area in the state after Boston and Barnstable. That size matters to sellers: a Taunton address can mean a downtown street near the Green, a lakeside lot, or a wooded parcel near the industrial park in the north.

The river has tributaries including the Mill River and the Three Mile River. The highest point is near the southwest corner, at 207 feet above sea level, and Prospect Hill above Lake Sabbatia reaches 197 feet.

What is Taunton's history?

Taunton was settled by English colonists in the late 1630s and incorporated as a town on September 3, 1639, which makes it one of the oldest towns in the country. It became a city in 1864 and was named for Taunton in Somerset, England.

The original boundaries took in land that is now Norton, Easton, Mansfield, Dighton, Raynham, Berkley and Lakeville. Elizabeth Poole, a financier of the first dam and ironworks, is described as the matriarch of the settlement, and the city motto, "Dux Femina Facti," means "A woman led the deed."

In the 1800s the city became known as the Silver City, because companies such as Reed & Barton, F. B. Rogers and Poole Silver made silverware here. Since December 1914 it has put on a large December light display on Taunton Green, which earned it the other nickname, the Christmas City.

What does Taunton's economy look like?

Taunton once ran on silversmithing and shipbuilding, and today leans toward manufacturing and industrial parks. Reed & Barton made the medals for the 1996 Summer Olympics, and the city produced the anchor for the USS Constitution.

Current descriptions emphasize semiconductor, silicon and electronics manufacturing, plus corporate headquarters, and the city has been courting biotechnology firms for its industrial parks. The Myles Standish Industrial Park in the north, next to Interstate 495, is the main one.

The Silver City Galleria mall closed on February 29, 2020 and was demolished on May 9, 2021, which reshaped retail in the area. Owners who sold or relocated for jobs in these industries sometimes need a fast, simple sale.

How do roads and transit work in Taunton?

Taunton is the highway hub of southeastern Massachusetts, and several major routes cross at the Green. U.S. 44, Route 138 and Route 140 meet there, Route 24 meets Route 140 near East Taunton, and Interstate 495 runs through the north.

The city has one MBTA Commuter Rail stop, East Taunton station. A proposed second phase of the South Coast Rail project would add a stop near downtown on Dean Street. The Greater Attleboro Taunton Regional Transit Authority (GATRA) runs local buses, and freight lines pass through the city.

Taunton has its own municipal airport for small aircraft. The nearest national airline service is T.F. Green Airport in Rhode Island, and the nearest international service is Logan in Boston.

  • Near the Green: walkable to downtown, courthouse and library
  • East Taunton: closest to the Commuter Rail and Route 24 or 140

What should you know about Taunton weather and the land?

Taunton has a humid climate with hot summers and cold winters, and it gets about 48.8 inches of precipitation a year. January days average a high near 38 degrees Fahrenheit, and July highs average about 84.

Snow averages 25.7 inches a year, mostly from December through March, and measurable precipitation falls on about 115 days a year. The city is built around a river with two state parks, Massasoit State Park in East Taunton and Watson Pond State Park in the north.

Because the city has rivers, ponds and low ground, a buyer for a lot near water may ask about flood zones and drainage. FEMA maps and the local conservation office hold that information, so check them for your own parcel.

What is downtown Taunton like?

Downtown Taunton centers on Taunton Green, the city's central square, which was a militia training ground during the Revolution. A fountain sits at its center, and the Liberty and Union flag flies beside the U.S. flag.

Nearby are the Taunton Public Library, which opened in 1903 and has been expanded several times, and the Old Colony Historical Society, which archives the city's past. The Bristol County Superior Courthouse and a trial court complex finished in 2011 keep county business in the city.

Architecture ranges from the colonial era to modern buildings. If your house is old, buyers may ask for a history of updates, so a short list of dates for the roof, heating and wiring is useful.

Which public schools serve Taunton?

Taunton operates nine public elementary schools, three middle schools and Taunton High School. The middle schools are Benjamin A. Friedman, Joseph H. Martin and John F. Parker.

The city also has Taunton Alternative High School and Bristol-Plymouth Regional Technical School, and Our Lady of Lourdes School in Weir Village for pre-K to grade 8. Family buyers often start with the school list, so having it ready helps your listing or private sale.

Before a Taunton sale closes, the fire department must issue a certificate of compliance for the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. State guidance says to call as soon as you set the closing date, and the inspection carries a local fee.

Which alarms are required depends on the year of construction and the last building permit. Alarms with no manufacture date are treated as expired, and old battery units must be replaced with sealed ten-year photoelectric models that have a hush button.

Revere in brief

Revere is a dense coastal city in Suffolk County, about five miles northeast of downtown Boston, and the end of the MBTA Blue Line. The 2020 census counted 62,186 people on 10.13 square miles, of which 4.43 square miles are water, so much of the city is marsh, beach and harbor edge. Winthrop, Chelsea, East Boston, Everett, Malden, Saugus and Lynn are the neighbors, with Massachusetts Bay to the east.

Roughly 10,900 people live on each square mile, so lots are tight and several districts mix single-family and multi-family houses. The census found 23,050 households and 24,539 housing units, 6.1 percent of them vacant. A homeowner vacancy rate of 0.6 percent means very few owner homes sat empty and for sale.

How the city grew

Revere began as Rumney Marsh, was part of Boston from 1632 and then Chelsea, and split off as North Chelsea in 1846. It took the name Revere in 1871 and became a city after a 1914 vote. Railroad lines, the Eastern Railroad in 1838 and the Boston, Revere Beach and Lynn Railroad in 1875, set off rapid growth. That first boom is when most of Revere filled in, so older houses are common.

Neighborhoods buyers ask about

Each district has a different housing mix, so name yours when you describe the house.

  • Beachmont: the eastern edge near East Boston's Orient Heights, with single and multi-family homes and a Blue Line stop.
  • Revere Beach Boulevard: apartment complexes, restaurants and some single-family houses along the three-mile beach, with newer development adding luxury apartments.
  • Point of Pines and Oak Island: the north end of the beach, mostly single and multi-family homes beside the marsh and wetlands.
  • Shirley Avenue: the most ethnically diverse part of the city, with ethnic groceries, restaurants and community services.
  • Broadway and Revere Street: the central civic and commercial arteries that connect City Hall to the beach.
  • West Revere: single and multi-family homes plus the Squire Road business district with large shopping plazas and hotels.

A beachfront condo and a West Revere two-family attract different people, so match the pitch to the district.

The Blue Line and roads

The Blue Line ends in Revere, with three stations: Wonderland, Revere Beach and Beachmont. Houses within walking distance of a station can be easier to market to commuters who work in Boston. U.S. Route 1 and state routes 1A, 16, 60, 107 and 145 run through the city.

When you list or sell, give the station name and the walking time. Buyers searching for a Blue Line home compare those details first. A new Revere High School is under construction at the former Wonderland Greyhound Park site, where ground was broken in August 2025, so the area around Wonderland is changing.

Storms, marsh and flood questions

Revere sits only about 20 feet above sea level, with marsh and ocean on several sides. Two events show why buyers watch storms: the Blizzard of 1978 destroyed many of the beach's remaining businesses, and an EF2 tornado came through Chelsea and into Revere on July 28, 2014, damaging many buildings, City Hall among them.

The year-round temperature range is roughly 23 to 82 degrees Fahrenheit, with snow lasting about five months and the muggiest stretch running from mid-June to late September. If your house is near the beach or the marsh, ask your insurer and the city building office about flood zone status before listing, so you know the answer before a buyer asks.

Before closing a Revere sale

State rules set the checklist. Your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms must pass a fire department inspection, and the department issues a certificate of compliance for the sale or transfer. Alarms more than ten years old, or with no date, have to be replaced. The department charges for the inspection, so call once a closing date is set. See the Mass.gov guidance.

Massachusetts also taxes deeds by statute. The base rate in G.L. c. 64D, section 1 is $2 per $500 of price, and your attorney can confirm the amount for your sale.

The assessors and exemptions

Revere's Assessors Department is at 281 Broadway. You can call 781-286-8170 or write to assessors@revere.org. The city lists senior, blind and hardship exemptions on its assessors page. Each requires ownership and occupancy, and if the property is in a trust the applicant must be both trustee and beneficiary or hold a life estate.

Ask the assessors whether an exemption on your bill affects the closing, and give the latest bill to your attorney.

If your assessment looks too high

  • Pay every tax installment on time. The Appellate Tax Board treats timely payment as a condition for hearing an appeal.
  • File an abatement application with the assessors by the first installment due date printed on your bill.
  • Wait up to three months for a decision, then appeal to the board within three months of that decision or of the deemed denial.
  • Bring comparable sales and photographs of similar nearby houses.

The burden is on the owner, so a short, evidence-based case does better than a general complaint. The board's guide explains each step.

A seller's checklist

A few steps in a sensible order save time on a Revere sale.

  • Pull your latest tax bill and call the assessors if an exemption is involved.
  • Check the age of every smoke and carbon monoxide alarm and replace the old ones.
  • Book the fire department inspection as soon as a closing date is set.
  • Write down anything you know about water, storm damage or flood zone status.
  • Give the deed, any mortgage payoff figure and estate paperwork to your attorney.

Houses here range from older mill-era and early twentieth century buildings to newer beachfront apartments, so condition varies a lot. Tight lots and shared walls in multi-family houses can also affect access for repairs and showings, which is one reason some owners prefer a single visit from a cash buyer to weeks of open houses.

Ways to sell a Revere house

A traditional listing, a sale on your own and a cash sale are the three routes. Which fits depends on repairs, timing and how much effort you can give.

  • A listing exposes the house to the most buyers but brings showings, inspection negotiations and a timeline set by the buyer's lender.
  • A cash sale can close on a schedule you choose, and the buyer takes the house in its present condition.

If your house needs work, a cash buyer may make more sense than spending months on repairs, and you can compare both routes before deciding. Cash Home Buyers can look at a Revere house as it stands, and the offer carries no obligation. Ask for a closing date that fits your plans, and keep the fire certificate and recording steps on your list whichever route you take. If tenants live in one unit of a multi-family house, say so at the start so everyone can plan around them.

The 2020 census counted 62,186 residents.

The Blue Line ends in Revere with stations at Wonderland, Revere Beach and Beachmont.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Revere?

Yes. The local fire department has to issue a certificate of compliance for a sale or transfer of a home.

Who handles property assessments in Revere?

The Assessors Department at 281 Broadway, reachable at 781-286-8170 or assessors@revere.org.

Medford at a glance

Just north of Boston, Medford is a Middlesex County city that the Mystic River crosses from west to southeast. It covers 8.66 square miles. The 2020 census counted 59,659 residents in 24,413 households and 25,770 housing units, with 5.3 percent vacant.

Part of the 2,060 acre Middlesex Fells Reservation lies in the north, shared with Winchester, Stoneham, Melrose and Malden. Tufts University has its campus along the Medford and Somerville line, mostly on Medford Hillside, and a steady student and staff population keeps the rental market active in nearby streets, which is worth knowing if you own a multi-family house on or near Medford Hillside. Landlords there often field offers from buyers who plan to keep renting the units.

Neighborhoods

People in Medford usually name their neighborhood first, and each has its own feel.

  • West Medford, described as the most affluent area, with a historic African American neighborhood dating to the Civil War.
  • South Medford, traditionally Italian.
  • Wellington, also called East Medford.
  • Fulton Heights, or The Heights, in North Medford.
  • Brooks Estates, Glenwood, Lawrence Estates and Medford Hillside, where Tufts is mostly situated.

For a listing or a private sale, the neighborhood name tells a buyer more about a house than the city name does, so use it.

Why many Medford homes are old

English colonists settled Medford in 1630 as part of Charlestown, and it became a city in 1892. The Boston and Maine Railroad reached Medford Center in 1847, and farmland was divided into house lots starting in the 1840s and 1850s, so many houses date from the 1800s and early 1900s.

Medford made tiles, crackers, bricks, rum and clipper ships, and the first toll bridge over the Mystic went up in 1637 where the Cradock Bridge stands today. Historic sites include the Peter Tufts House at 350 Riverside Avenue, thought to be the oldest all-brick building in New England. Houses in the old Ship Street Historic District around Riverside Avenue are some of the oldest, and an old house can mean old systems.

Transit

Medford has both Orange Line and Green Line subway service, plus a commuter rail stop and many bus routes.

ServiceWhere in Medford

Interstate 93 runs north and south through the city, and state routes 16, 28, 38 and 60 cross it. Houses close to the new Green Line stops sit in a part of the city where transit changed recently, which can matter to buyers of all kinds.

Selling a rental or an inherited house

Landlords sometimes decide to sell after repeated turnover, damage or a change in family plans. A cash buyer can take a house with tenants or one left empty, so say which yours is.

If you inherited a house, you may need probate steps before you can sell, depending on how it was held. Speak with a Massachusetts attorney about that first, then share the address and condition with a buyer. Often the sale can go forward as soon as whoever holds authority to sell has it, and a cash buyer will usually wait while that is settled.

Fire department certificate

Before a Medford sale can close, the fire department must certify your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.

Owners are told to find the year the house was built and the date of its last building permit, make a list of every alarm with its manufacture date, and replace any that are expired or undated. Battery smoke alarms past 10 years need sealed 10 year photoelectric replacements with a hush feature. Test the new units, then call the fire department, which charges a fee for the inspection and certificate.

Deed excise and recording

The deed excise under Chapter 64D, Section 1 is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of price or fraction of it, outside Barnstable County. Deeds are recorded at a county registry. Medford's county, Middlesex, has a South registry in Cambridge and a North registry in Lowell.

Ask Medford's city offices about permits, open violations and any tax bills before you close. Your contract and attorney will say who pays the excise.

How a cash sale works

Because a cash buyer is not waiting on a mortgage lender, the closing date can follow your needs.

  1. You give the address, condition, any tenants and your timing.
  2. The buyer looks the house over and sends a written offer.
  3. You accept, and an attorney takes over title work and the purchase and sale agreement.
  4. The alarm certificate and payoff letters are lined up.
  5. The deed is recorded and you receive the proceeds.

Ask any buyer how they reach their number, since an offer should reflect the house itself. Then compare the net result with listing, counting repairs, showings and months of carrying costs.

What a cash sale skips

With no lender there is no bank appraisal, no loan commitment and no financing contingency that can unravel days before closing. Showings shrink to a visit or two, and nobody asks you to repaint, patch the roof or empty every closet first.

State requirements remain. The alarm certificate, title search, payoff letters and deed recording still happen, and your attorney still reviews the contract. What disappears is the lender's schedule, which is where many conventional sales lose weeks.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Papers to gather first

Gather the newest tax bill, any water balance, a mortgage payoff statement, lease copies and receipts for big repairs. For estate property, add the papers that show who may sign the deed. A complete folder lets a buyer commit to a price and a closing date you can count on, and it saves your attorney from chasing documents in the final week.

From accepted offer to closing

Once you accept, the attorney orders a title search that lists mortgages, liens and unpaid charges, and each is paid off or released. The alarm inspection is booked, and the deed is prepared for the registry. At closing you sign the deed and settlement statement, your lenders are paid from the proceeds, and you receive the balance.

With no lender approval to wait on, the usual delays in a Medford sale are an old lien and an alarm check booked too late. Start both the week the contract is signed. Ask for the closing date and the alarm certificate responsibility in writing, and keep copies of every payoff letter. If a tenant lives in the house, tell the buyer when the lease ends so the sale and the move line up.

Yes. Wellington is on the Orange Line, and Medford/Tufts and Ball Square are on the Green Line, which opened in 2022. West Medford has Lowell Line commuter rail.

Yes. A certificate of compliance from the local fire department is required when you sell or transfer a home. Call the Medford fire department for the fee and scheduling.

What is the deed excise tax when I sell in Medford?

It is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of the sale price or fraction of it. Your contract and attorney will confirm which party pays.

Where is Weymouth, MA, and what are its four villages?

Weymouth is a Norfolk County city on the South Shore, bordered by Hingham Bay and Boston Harbor to the north. It covers 21.58 square miles, but 4.81 of that is water, and the 2020 Census counted 57,437 residents.

Residents describe four districts. North Weymouth sits north of the Church, North and Green Street junction and has the waterfront parks and beaches. South Weymouth lies mostly south of Route 3 and holds Weymouth High School and South Shore Hospital. East Weymouth has Whitman's Pond, Jackson Square and Town Hall, plus many Victorian houses. Weymouth Landing spans about a mile around Weston Park at the Braintree line.

Quincy, Braintree and Holbrook lie to the west, Abington and Rockland to the south, and Hingham to the east. Grape Island, Slate Island and Sheep Island in the Boston Harbor Islands National Recreation Area also belong to Weymouth.

What is Weymouth's history?

Weymouth began in 1622 as the Wessagusset colony, which makes it the second-oldest settlement in Massachusetts after Plymouth. The first attempt failed, but settlers who stayed formed the base of the permanent town, which took the Weymouth name in 1635.

Shoemaking was the main industry from the early 1700s until Stetson Shoe closed in 1973. The old Naval Air Station South Weymouth closed in the 1990s, and the land is being redeveloped as Union Point. Weymouth also voted in 1999 to replace town meeting with a mayor and council, ending 365 years of continuous town meeting. The first mayor took office in 2000.

How do Weymouth's waterfront and climate affect homes?

Water shapes much of Weymouth, from Hingham Bay to the Back River and Fore River. The city is especially vulnerable to sea level rise. It also describes North Weymouth waterfront cottages being bought and rebuilt, so condition and flood exposure vary a great deal from street to street.

Average precipitation runs about 44 inches a year, with January highs near 39 degrees. If you own near the shore:

  • Pull your flood insurance policy and any elevation certificate.
  • Document sea wall, bulkhead or drainage repairs with dates.
  • Tell buyers or the cash buyer about past water in the basement.

Put the history in writing for any buyer, since hiding it tends to surface at inspection.

What is the East Weymouth housing like, and what do older houses need?

East Weymouth has many Queen Anne, shingle and colonial revival houses, with restoration under way on streets such as Hillcrest Road. Whatever the village, it is worth having the roof, heating system, wiring and porches looked at before you decide how to sell.

The city's 2010 housing count showed 64 percent owner-occupied and 35 percent renter-occupied, so renters live in a large share of the housing. If you inherited one of these houses and live elsewhere, a repair list can be the biggest hurdle to a traditional listing.

Which schools and roads serve Weymouth?

Weymouth High School in South Weymouth is the city's only public high school and enrolls more than 1,800 students. The Maria Weston Chapman Middle School opened in September 2022, and eight primary schools and an early childhood center complete the system. Private options include South Shore Christian Academy and the Catholic Sacred Heart and St. Francis Xavier schools.

Routes 3, 3A, 18, 53, 58 and 139 pass through the city. The MBTA Greenbush Line stops at East Weymouth and Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, and the Kingston Line stops at South Weymouth. If your house is within reach of a station, say so in any listing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Weymouth houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What is Union Point, and what else is around Weymouth?

Union Point is the redevelopment of the former Naval Air Station South Weymouth. Plans for a parkway, residences, a sports facility and a movie studio, and notes the site has hosted several film shoots. The 25-acre Union Point Sports Complex is already open.

700 acres of parks and conservation land across 46 sites. North Weymouth has Great Esker Park, George Lane Beach and Webb Memorial State Park, and in spring hundreds of thousands of alewife herring run up the brook between the Back River and Whitman's Pond. Abigail Adams was born in Weymouth, and her birthplace is a local landmark.

How do Massachusetts property tax abatements work for Weymouth owners?

Weymouth assessors follow the state process explained by the Appellate Tax Board. You can seek an abatement if the assessed value is above the fair cash value as of the January 1 valuation date, or if an exemption or classification applies.

  • Bills in quarterly cities are generally due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.
  • The abatement application is due by the first installment date, generally February 1 in those cities.
  • Assessors have three months, and no answer counts as a denial.
  • You then have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Weymouth's assessing office publishes its own schedule. Ask it which billing pattern applies and where to get the abatement form.

What does a Weymouth seller pay to record the deed?

Weymouth deeds are recorded with the Norfolk County Registry of Deeds. The registry charges $156 to record a deed and an excise tax of $2.28 for each $500 of the stated price. Its own example shows a $155,000 deed owing $706.80, and the excise must be paid with an attorney's check or bank check.

On a $600,000 sale the same rate gives $2,736. A municipal lien certificate costs $81 at the registry, and a mortgage discharge is $106 per marginal reference, so budget for these small items too.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Cash sale versus listing for a Weymouth house

A Weymouth listing can draw plenty of attention, particularly near the commuter rail, but showings and repairs take time. A cash sale suits owners who want to close on their own schedule, who inherited a house, or who face a repair bill they do not want to carry.

Ask any buyer for proof of funds, a written contract and a clear statement of who pays each closing cost. Then compare the net you would keep from each option.

Frequently asked questions

Is Weymouth, MA a city or a town?

Weymouth has a city form of government but keeps "Town of Weymouth" as its official name. Voters replaced town meeting with a mayor and council in 1999.

How many train stations are in Weymouth?

Three. The Greenbush Line stops at East Weymouth and Weymouth Landing/East Braintree, and the Kingston Line stops at South Weymouth.

How much is the deed excise tax in Norfolk County?

The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds charges $2.28 for each $500 of the stated price or fraction of $500, payable by attorney's check or bank check at recording.

Which parts of Weymouth are near the water?

North Weymouth faces Hingham Bay and Boston Harbor. The Back River and Fore River also run through the city, so check flood exposure street by street.

What happened to the Naval Air Station in South Weymouth?

It closed in the 1990s under the Base Realignment and Closure process, and the land is being redeveloped as Union Point, a mixed-use community with homes, a sports complex and film production space.

Can I sell my Weymouth house as is?

Yes. You can sell as is to an investor or cash buyer. Disclose known problems in writing, and expect the offer to reflect the repairs the house needs.

Peabody and its housing

Peabody is an Essex County city on the North Shore, about 15 miles northeast of Boston and 2 miles from the center of Salem. It covers 16.81 square miles, shaped like a wedge, with the center at the wider northeastern end. South Peabody lies below the center, and the more suburban West Peabody, where the high school sits, is out past the highways and the Proctor neighborhood. Middleton, Danvers, Salem, Lynn and Lynnfield border it.

The 2020 census counted 54,481 residents in 22,315 households and 23,191 housing units, with 3.8% of units vacant. The population doubled between 1950 and 1970, from 22,645 to 48,080, so a large share of homes date from that postwar growth. About 24.2% of residents are 65 or older, and older owners and estates are a steady source of local sales.

Reaching the assessors

Call the assessors at 978-538-5716. Before a sale, ask two things. Does an exemption on your bill end when the property transfers? And does the cyclical inspection program have a visit scheduled for your address? A pending inspection can change the record on your house, and a buyer may ask about it.

Share the current bill with any buyer's attorney so closing adjustments make sense, and ask the assessors how an exemption you hold is treated after the transfer.

Low ground near the rivers

The Ipswich River forms the northwestern border, and the Waters River drains the northeast. Low-lying lots near those waterways deserve a flood question before you sell, so check your status with your insurer and the city building office and write down anything you know about wet basements.

Peabody has useful green space that buyers often ask about: Independence Greenway, a 5.25 mile rail trail, and Brooksby Farm, a 275-acre city-owned farm and conservation area. Crystal Lake, a 21-acre conservation area, is another local landmark. If your house sits in a designated historic district, such as the Washington Street Historic District, ask the city whether any local rules apply.

Older houses and what buyers check

Peabody was settled in 1626 as part of Salem and became a city in 1916. Leather made the city's name for generations, and it is still called the Leather City, but the tanneries have closed or moved. A big share of the housing was added during the postwar boom, when the population doubled in twenty years.

Houses of similar age tend to need the same work at about the same time: roofs, boilers, wiring and windows. A buyer's inspector will list those items, and a lender may ask for repairs before it releases funds. That is the situation where owners weigh an as-is sale against a repair project. West Peabody, mostly farm land until the 1950s, has newer houses than the area around the center, so age and condition vary by section.

Electric service and getting around

The Peabody Municipal Light Plant, owned by the city, provides electricity, so transferring electric service to a new owner runs through a city utility, which is different from most Massachusetts towns. National Grid supplies natural gas, and Comcast and RCN hold cable licenses.

Highways include Interstate 95, Route 128, Route 129, U.S. Route 1 and Route 114. Several MBTA bus lines pass through town. There is no commuter rail station in the city, and the closest stop is in Salem on the Newburyport/Rockport Line to North Station. The nearest airports are Beverly Municipal and Boston's Logan.

Start with the fire department. A Peabody seller needs an alarm certificate, and state fire officials advise calling for the inspection as soon as a closing date exists and expecting a fee. The Department of Fire Services explains the steps.

An attorney handles the closing and the recorded deed, since attorneys are part of Massachusetts sales by law and by practice. The deed excise is set by Chapter 64D, Section 1. Sellers of certain residential properties also cannot make an offer conditional on a waiver of a home inspection under 760 CMR 74.

A direct purchase follows the same legal path. You may still need to clear a mortgage payoff, estate paperwork or a lien before the deed records.

Order of work for a Peabody sale

A sale moves faster when you do the slow items first.

  • Request your tax and assessment information from the assessors and note any exemption.
  • Find your home's build date and last permit date, then check the age of every smoke and carbon monoxide alarm.
  • Set a closing date and call the fire department for the inspection, expecting a fee.
  • Ask your lender for a payoff figure if a mortgage remains, and collect estate paperwork if heirs are selling.
  • Give everything to your attorney, who handles the closing and the recorded deed.

If the house is in the Washington Street Historic District or another designated area, add one more call to the city about local rules before you commit to repairs or a closing date.

Neighborhoods buyers mention

Buyers describe Peabody by section, so use those names in your description.

  • The center and Peabody Square in the northeast.
  • South Peabody, with Tillie's Farm, a city-owned farm.
  • West Peabody, home to the high school.
  • The Proctor neighborhood between the center and the west.

West Peabody was mostly farm land until the 1950s and has since grown into a residential area, so houses there tend to be newer than those near the center.

Whichever section you are in, name it clearly when you talk to buyers, and mention the nearest highway access and bus lines, since commuters to Boston make up much of the local market. Ask your agent or attorney about parking and access too.

  • Estates in which heirs live out of state.

  • Owners facing a move on a short schedule.

Tell us what the house needs and who has to sign, and we can describe how an offer would line up with those documents. Before you call, gather the deed, the latest tax bill, any payoff letter and, for an estate, the paperwork showing who has authority. With those in hand the closing timeline gets shorter, and you can compare the offer with the cost and delay of repairs and showings.

What are Peabody's property tax rates?

The FY26 rates are $9.47 residential and $18.85 commercial, Check the unit and your own bill with the assessors.

Call the Assessors Office at 978-538-5716. Its page also links to exemption information and a cyclical inspection FAQ.

Yes. The city-owned Peabody Municipal Light Plant provides electricity, while National Grid provides natural gas.

Is there commuter rail in Peabody?

No station is in the city. The nearest commuter rail service is in Salem on the Newburyport/Rockport Line.

Chicopee's villages and housing

Chicopee is a Hampden County city on the Connecticut River, the second largest in western Massachusetts after Springfield. The 2020 census counted 55,560 residents across about 23.9 square miles. It began as a cluster of mill villages and broke away from Springfield in 1848, and each village kept its own center and its own style of house.

  • Chicopee Center, also called Cabotville
  • Chicopee Falls
  • Willimansett
  • Fairview
  • Aldenville
  • Burnett Road, Smith Highlands and Westover

A seller in Willimansett and a seller in Fairview deal with different streets, lot sizes and house ages, so a citywide rule of thumb rarely fits. Name the village when you describe the house. Buyers search by neighborhood feel as much as by address, and a clear village name saves a round of questions.

Why so many older, modest houses?

Mill owners built housing for workers, and that is why dense streets of two-family and single-family homes stand near the old factories. Textile companies set up along the Chicopee River between 1823 and 1841. In Aldenville, a developer bought 600 acres east of Willimansett in 1870 and cut it into small lots for factory workers, so houses there are often more than a century old.

Buyers know what that means: old wiring, older heating systems and possibly lead paint. Be ready for those questions. Decide early whether to fix issues first or sell as is, and write down what you have replaced and when, since a dated record of a new furnace or panel reassures a cautious buyer.

Highways and commuting

Four interstates cross Chicopee: I-90, I-91, I-291 and I-391. State routes 33, 116 and 141 also run through it. Hartford is about 29 miles away and Boston about 89. Springfield, Holyoke and Hartford are quick drives, which widens the buyer pool beyond people who work in the city.

A house near an interstate ramp can show well on commute time but may carry road noise. Buyers notice both, so mention the drive times that help you and be candid about the traffic sound if a visit will reveal it anyway. Photos taken on a quiet weekday morning do not replace an honest description.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Chicopee house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Flood risk and wet basements

Chicopee sits between two rivers. The Willimansett Dike, a levee in Willimansett, was built after the flood from the Great New England Hurricane of 1938.

A house near the Chicopee or Connecticut River may need a flood zone check, and a buyer's lender can require flood insurance. Ask your insurance agent or the city for your parcel's zone before you list. Basements in older mill-village homes can also run damp, which inspectors tend to flag. If yours has taken on water, tell buyers plainly.

Property tax abatement steps

Abatement stepTime limit
Apply to the Chicopee assessorsDue date of the first installment, typically February 1 under quarterly billing
Assessors decideThree months, and silence counts as a denial
Appeal to the Appellate Tax BoardWithin three months of the decision or deemed denial

Chicopee elects three assessors to three-year terms, and they handle these requests. Use the approved form. You generally have to pay the tax by its due date for the Board to hear an appeal. Call the assessors for the form and your bill's actual due dates.

If you are selling, an abatement can still matter because the buyer inherits the assessment going forward.

What the state requires before closing

Chicopee's fire department must certify that your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale standard. The state Department of Fire Services suggests calling as soon as a closing date exists. The inspection costs a fee. Any battery smoke alarm past ten years, or lacking a manufacture date, has to come out for a sealed ten-year photoelectric model with a hush button. Waiting until the final week risks a late closing.

A state excise tax under chapter 64D of the General Laws attaches to the deed, based on the price. Your closing attorney computes it and tells you who pays under your contract. A mortgage payoff or unpaid city bills are settled at the same table.

How to sell: three routes compared

  • Listing with an agent suits a sound house and a patient seller. Plan for showings, repair requests, agent fees and a lender's timeline.
  • Selling by owner fits someone who knows the street and can handle contracts. Plan for pricing, marketing, paperwork and negotiations.
  • A cash buyer suits a fixer-upper, an inherited home, or a seller working to a fixed date. The offer reflects condition, so compare it with a listing estimate.

Inherited houses, mill-era two-families with tenants and homes with deferred repairs are common in Chicopee. Cash Home Buyers takes a house in whatever state it is in, so the paint, the roof patch and the cluttered basement can stay as they are. Request an offer, lay it beside the other routes, and choose by your calendar.

Questions to answer before listing

Sit down with a pen before you pick a route. How soon do you need the money? What would a buyer's inspector flag in the basement, roof and heating? Does anyone else have a say, such as a sibling, a co-owner or a tenant? Do you owe back taxes or a mortgage balance? Your answers point to the route that fits, and they may reveal a deadline you had not noticed, and they give you the facts any buyer, agent or attorney will ask for first.

Common snags for Chicopee sellers

  • Aging systems in houses that date from the mill years
  • Tenants in two-family homes who complicate showings
  • Estate sales where several relatives must agree
  • Smoke and CO inspection timing right before closing

Whatever the issue, start with the facts about your house and a clear date you want to close by.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Tenants, estates and the days before closing

With a tenant in place, read the lease and tell your buyer about the rent and the end date early. Tenants keep their rights through a sale, and a Massachusetts attorney can advise you if you want a tenant to leave. For an estate, every heir has to agree before the house is sold, so get the family on one page and talk to an attorney about probate before you accept an offer.

In the last stretch, book the fire inspection, confirm the tax balance with the city, and gather the deed and recent bills for your closing attorney. A seller who has these items in order gets to the closing table without scrambling, and a calm closing day is worth the effort of an early start, for you and for the buyer.

How big is Chicopee and how many people live there?

About 23.9 square miles in Hampden County, with 55,560 residents at the 2020 census.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell a house in Chicopee?

Yes. Before a Chicopee home changes hands, the fire department has to sign off on your alarms. Phone it once closing is scheduled; a fee applies, and aging alarms may need swapping out.

Can I sell a Chicopee house that has tenants?

Yes, but tenants' rights stay in place and the sale can affect timing. Tell your buyer about leases and rent early.

Does Chicopee have flood risk that affects a sale?

Parts of the city sit near the Chicopee and Connecticut Rivers. Check your parcel's flood zone, since a lender may require flood insurance.

How do I challenge my Chicopee property tax assessment?

Your application goes to the Chicopee assessors, and the deadline is the first installment's due date, which is typically February 1 for quarterly bills. A denial can be taken to the state Appellate Tax Board within three months.

Rates change from year to year, so the number on your own bill is the one that counts. Buyers and their attorneys usually ask for the latest bill, and having it ready saves a day or two.

The assessor and your property tax

Values are redone every five years under state law, and the Department of Revenue certifies them before the rate is set. The assessing office also handles abatement applications, exemptions for seniors, disabled persons, surviving spouses and blind persons, and reassessments after a building permit is issued.

  • Office: Searles Building, Room 103, 41 Pleasant Street
  • Phone: 978-983-8530
  • Email: assessor@methuen.gov

If you pulled a permit for a deck, an addition or a finished basement, expect the value on the card to reflect it. Forms and contacts are on the Methuen assessing page.

Does the historic district affect a sale?

Possibly, depending on your address. Methuen set up the Searles Tenney Nevins Historic District in 1992, and owners inside it follow the Historic District Commission's rules on materials, building size and proportions, and colors. Violations can lead to fines and other legal action.

The Spicket Falls Historic District and the Pleasant-High Historic District sit inside the larger area, and both are on the National Register of Historic Places. If your house is in this part of the city, find out whether earlier exterior work went through the commission, since a buyer's attorney may ask. Check with the city on whether your address falls inside the boundary before you list or sell.

Rivers, ponds and flood questions

Methuen runs along the northern bank of the Merrimack River, and the Spicket River divides the city in two. There are also brooks, several ponds, a town forest, a bird sanctuary and Tenney State Park.

Forest Lake is a great pond of more than 55 acres next to the town forest, and the Forest Lake Association manages access. Pine Island sits in the Merrimack near the southern edge of the city and belongs to Methuen. A house near any of this water can bring up drainage, flood zone and insurance questions, and a buyer's lender or inspector may raise them. Gather what you know about wet basements or past flooding before you list.

Getting around Methuen

Methuen sits at the northern end of Interstate 93 in Massachusetts, with three exits serving the city. Interstate 495 crosses the eastern side, and Route 213, the Loop Connector, links the two highways. Routes 28, 110 and 113 also pass through.

  • Boston is a 25 to 30 minute drive, and Manchester, New Hampshire is about 25 minutes.
  • The Merrimack Valley Regional Transit Authority runs the local buses.
  • OurBus runs service to Worcester and New York City from the Methuen Park and Ride.
  • The nearest MBTA commuter rail stops are Lawrence, Bradford and Haverhill on the Haverhill/Reading Line.

Commuters are a big part of the buyer pool, so mention the highway exits and the drive times when you describe the house.

Steps before a Methuen closing

Expect three fixtures in a Methuen sale: the fire department's sign-off on your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, a title search and a real estate attorney.

  • Book the fire department visit the moment a closing date is set. The checklist it applies varies with the year the house went up and when the last permit was pulled.
  • Old battery-only smoke alarms get replaced by sealed 10-year photoelectric models that include a hush button.
  • The deed is filed at a county registry of deeds. Most Massachusetts parcels, about 80 to 90 percent, are recorded land. The remainder is registered land handled through the Land Court.
  • The state charges a deeds excise under Chapter 64D, Section 1. Your attorney can give you the current amount.

A cash purchase from Cash Home Buyers does not remove any of these. The buyer takes the house as it stands, and the paperwork still runs through the fire department, the registry and your attorney.

Selling an older Methuen house

Plenty of owners here hold mill-era housing, an inherited property or a house in need of repairs. A home built in the early 1900s may need alarm upgrades, repairs an inspector flagged or old permit records pulled before a buyer will close.

Homes in the historic district carry extra rules for exterior changes, and houses near the Spicket or the Merrimack may draw drainage questions. A cash offer can shorten the wait for a buyer's financing. The municipal and state steps stay the same, so it helps to start the fire department call and the tax bill request early.

A practical order of work looks like this. First, get your latest tax bill and confirm your address against the historic district boundary. Second, call the fire department about the alarm certificate once a closing date is set. Third, give your attorney the deed, any permit records and notes on past water problems. Fourth, review the offer and the closing date that fit your plans, and say no to anything that does not.

Cash sale: what falls away and what stays

With a cash buyer there is no mortgage underwriting, no appraisal waiting on a lender and no financing contingency that can fall through late. You do not need to stage the house, schedule showings or fix what an inspector would have listed.

What stays: the title search, the recorded deed, the fire department certificate and the deeds excise. If taxes are owed, the balance is settled from the sale proceeds at the table, so ask the assessing office and your attorney where you stand before you sign. Bring the deed, your latest tax bill and any permit paperwork to your first call, and the whole thing moves faster.

Methuen is in Essex County, Massachusetts, along the New Hampshire border, in the Merrimack Valley.

What is the Methuen property tax rate?

For FY2026 the residential rate is $10.40 per $1,000 of value and the commercial rate is $20.08. Rates are set again each fiscal year.

Is a smoke detector certificate required to sell in Methuen?

Yes. A sale or transfer needs a compliance certificate from the local fire department, which charges a fee. Call to schedule once a closing date is set.

Is there a historic district in Methuen?

Yes. The city created the Searles Tenney Nevins Historic District in 1992, and a commission regulates exterior changes inside it. Ask the city whether your address is within the boundary.

Can I sell a Methuen house as is?

Yes, you can sell with repairs undone. You still need the fire department certificate and clear title, and your attorney can advise on open permits and tax balances.

Everett housing market basics

Everett is a small, dense Middlesex County city directly north of Boston, next to the Charlestown neighborhood. About 3.7 square miles hold 49,075 residents, roughly 14,364 people per square mile, so houses sit close together on small lots. Most of the housing is on tight streets near Broadway, with industrial land along the water.

People look for homes here to stay near downtown Boston without paying Boston, Cambridge or Somerville living costs, and the population has been climbing. Compact houses, two-families and triple-deckers are the norm.

Getting around: roads and transit

Route 16 crosses the southern part of the city and links to U.S. Route 1 and Interstate 93, which both run just outside the city limits.

What is being built nearby?

  • The former Exxon tank site was sold for cleanup and redevelopment, starting with raising the land and adding apartment buildings near Route 16, and Exxon agreed to a deed restriction barring fossil fuel storage there.
  • A 700 megawatt, four-hour battery received approval from the Energy Facilities Siting Board.
  • MassDOT is designing a bike and pedestrian bridge from the Encore harborwalk to Somerville's Draw Seven park.
  • The New England Revolution have plans for a soccer stadium in the city.

Construction can mean noise and truck traffic near the Mystic River for years. None of it changes what your own house is worth on a given day, but you should be able to say what is going on nearby.

Is flooding a concern for an Everett house?

Everett is low-lying, at an average elevation of about 10 feet, with a long waterfront on the Mystic River. The redevelopment plan for the old tank site includes raising the land to avoid climate-related flooding.

Expect a lender or buyer to want your lot's flood zone, and expect an inspector to notice a basement that has been wet. Check the zone and keep repair and insurance records where you can find them.

Deed tax and fire certificate

Chapter 64D of the General Laws puts an excise tax on the deed. It is measured on the price, leaving out any loan that stays on the property. Your closing attorney calculates it.

Everett's fire department also has to certify your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Book the visit the moment a closing date exists. It costs a fee, and the state's fire services office advises not to wait. Replace tired alarms before the inspector shows up.

Everett property tax is billed separately from the sale. Where a Massachusetts community bills quarterly, installments usually fall on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1, and an abatement request must be filed by the first one. Read your own bill for the exact dates.

Call the Everett assessors if you think your house is overvalued, and bring comparable sales. Any balance still owing is taken from your proceeds at the closing table, so get the number before you settle on a price.

Selling with tenants, liens or repairs

Many Everett owners hold a two-family or a three-decker where one unit is rented. Before you list, gather each lease, note the rent and the end date, and check that the permits for past work are in order. Tenants keep their rights through a sale, and showings need their cooperation.

Liens and unpaid balances come out at closing, so find them early. A house that needs repairs can be fixed and listed, or sold as is, and the right choice depends on how much money and time you have.

What are the ways to sell an Everett house?

You have three common routes: list, sell by owner, or take a cash offer. A cash sale tends to appeal when time matters or the house needs work.

  • A listing can reach many buyers but involves showings and repair requests.
  • A sale by owner saves a fee but puts the work on you.
  • A cash buyer takes the house as is and can close when you want.

Preparing the house and the file

Everett lots are small, so first impressions come from the street. Clear the entry, tidy the yard and the walkway, and fix anything a visitor sees right away, like a loose railing or a broken window. Inside, a clean, empty basement helps an inspector and a buyer see what is there.

Then build the file: deed, recent tax bills, permit records, leases, any repair receipts and the fire department certificate once you have it. A seller who can hand a buyer's attorney a folder in one afternoon often keeps a deal on schedule.

A note on timing

Closings in a city this dense often hinge on small items: a lien that needs a payoff letter, a tenant who needs notice, an inspection date that slipped. List each one on a single page with a date next to it. If you are working against a deadline, such as a move, an estate settlement or a mortgage that is behind, tell every party the date up front so they can plan around it. A cash sale gives you the most control over timing, while a listing depends on a buyer's lender and inspection schedule.

Before you accept any offer

Insist on a written offer, and read who pays which closing costs. Confirm the closing date and ask whether the buyer needs financing or inspections first. Then call the assessors for your tax balance and the fire department for an inspection date, so you know your net before you say yes. If a number looks wrong, ask your closing attorney to check it. Compare at least two options, even if one is a simple listing estimate, and take your time reading the terms. A fair offer will still look fair after a night's sleep and a call to your attorney.

Middlesex County, directly north of Boston and next to the Charlestown neighborhood.

Do I need a smoke detector inspection to sell in Everett?

Yes. Everett's fire department signs off on smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before a sale. Call when you have a date.

Who pays the deed excise tax on a Massachusetts sale?

It is levied on the deed under chapter 64D of the General Laws, measured by the price. Your purchase contract usually decides who pays, so check with your attorney.

Can I sell an Everett house that needs repairs?

Yes. Either repair and list, or sell as is to a cash buyer. Compare repair cost and time with the offer.

Barnstable and its villages

Barnstable is the county seat of Barnstable County and the largest community on Cape Cod by land area and population, roughly 70 miles southeast of Boston. Cape Cod Bay forms its northern edge and Nantucket Sound its southern edge.

The town is a group of villages with no legal boundaries of their own. These seven are the ones most often listed:

  • Barnstable village, which includes Cummaquid
  • Centerville
  • Cotuit
  • Hyannis, which includes Hyannis Port and West Hyannisport
  • Marstons Mills
  • Osterville
  • West Barnstable

Most residents live in the south, many near the beaches of Centerville and Hyannis Harbors. Hyannis, the biggest village, is the commercial center of the Cape, with Cape Cod Hospital, Barnstable Municipal Airport and the ferries to Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard. Route 6 runs across town as a four lane freeway, and the nearest year-round commuter rail is at Middleborough and Kingston, so a commute to Boston is mostly a drive.

Town or city?

Barnstable swapped selectmen and town meeting for a council and town manager in 1989. Thirteen Massachusetts municipalities have a city government but keep "the town of" in the name, and Barnstable is among them. For paperwork, go to Town Hall at 367 Main Street in Hyannis.

Cape weather and your roof

Roughly 30 inches of snow falls from November through April, with February the worst and nor'easters at their peak. Inspectors for buyers tend to start with the roof and heating.

With a cash buyer those repairs are optional. Storm damage to a roof or deck does not block a sale.

Due dates and the Collector

Real estate tax comes in four quarterly payments per fiscal year. Preliminary bills one and two come due in early August and early November. Bills three and four are actual bills, due on these fiscal 2027 dates:

BillDue date
Third quarter (actual bill)February 1, 2027
Fourth quarter (actual bill)May 3, 2027

The actual bills are to be mailed by December 31, 2026. The Collector bills other items too: motor vehicle and boat excise, sewer usage, and betterments for roads, water, sewer and septic. A betterment attaches to the property, so tell your closing attorney about any you know of.

A municipal lien certificate request form is on the Collector's page, and your attorney can say if your sale needs one. Tax Collections answers at 508-862-4054.

Contesting your assessment

A value that looks too high calls for an abatement application to the assessors. Quarterly-billing towns generally set the cutoff at February 1, and appeals then go to the Appellate Tax Board. Keep paying installments while the request is open.

Septic and Title 5 inspections

A house on septic usually needs an inspection when it sells. State Title 5 rules call for one in the two years before the sale, or in the six months after if weather got in the way. Barnstable bills for sewer and for septic betterments, so some addresses are on sewer and some are not. Find out which applies to yours.

  • The inspector must be MassDEP approved, and the report is filed on the state form within 30 days.
  • Give the buyer a copy of the report.
  • A pass lasts two years in general, or three if the system is pumped every year and the records are in the report.
  • A conditional pass can cover a cracked tank or broken pipe. Cesspools and soil absorption systems cannot be fixed that way.
  • A failed system has to be upgraded within two years unless the Board of Health sets another schedule.

Transfers among spouses, parents and children, or full siblings are exempt, along with some trust and estate planning transfers. A buyer can also sign a binding agreement with the Board of Health to upgrade or tie into sewer within two years.

Deed excise tax

The state taxes a deed when it is recorded. For Barnstable County the statute's rate is below the one for the rest of the state: $1.50 per $500 of consideration or fraction of it. The registry sets recording fees on its own schedule, so your closing attorney can tell you what applies.

Before you close

Plan for three things when you sell a one or two family home.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. The fire department issues a certificate of compliance once your alarms pass. Phone it when a closing date is set, and expect a fee. Battery alarms past ten years get replaced with sealed ten year photoelectric units.
  • An attorney. Closings here count as legal work, so hire one early.
  • Title system. Most land is recorded at the Registry of Deeds. Some parcels are registered land, which carries a Land Court certificate of title.

One more rule: for certain residential properties, a seller cannot make an offer depend on the buyer waiving a home inspection.

Betterments and sewer charges

Cape houses often carry charges that a mainland seller never sees. A betterment is a charge for roads, water, sewer or septic work, and it stays with the property. Sewer usage is billed separately from the tax bill. Before you list, ask the Collector whether any betterment is open and whether it will be paid off at closing or passed to the buyer.

Vacant seasonal houses add another wrinkle. A house that sat empty through a Cape winter may have roof, heating or plumbing damage, and it may have an old septic system nobody has inspected. Get the inspection scheduled early, since a failed system can reshape the whole sale, and a buyer who plans to upgrade must sign an agreement with the Board of Health.

Write down what you learn from each office, with dates, and give the list to your attorney. It saves a round of phone calls at the end.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

From decision to closing

  1. Call the Collector at 508-862-4054 for your balance and any betterment on the property.
  2. Find out whether the house is on sewer or septic. If septic, line up an approved inspector.
  3. Choose a closing attorney and share the tax and betterment details.
  4. Schedule the fire department alarm certificate as soon as a date is set.
  5. At closing the deed is recorded, the excise tax is paid, and any tax balance comes out of your proceeds.

Selling as-is to Cash Home Buyers keeps repairs off the list, but the septic report, the alarm certificate and the tax payoff still apply. Ask us how each one will be handled when you request an offer.

Village by village differences

Seven villages mean seven different settings, from harbor streets in Hyannis to the wooded interior near Wequaquet Lake. A house in Cotuit and a house in West Barnstable can have very different sewer, water and tax situations, so confirm the details with the Collector and the Board of Health instead of assuming.

If the house needs septic work, carries a betterment, or sat vacant through a Cape winter, a direct sale can spare you the repair bills and the wait for an inspector. Cash Home Buyers buys Barnstable houses as they are.

Frequently asked questions

Is Barnstable a town or city?

It is both. The name stays Town of Barnstable, but a council and town manager charter has governed since 1989.

How many villages are in Barnstable?

Seven are commonly listed: Barnstable, Centerville, Cotuit, Hyannis, Marstons Mills, Osterville and West Barnstable. They have no legal boundaries.

When is the next Barnstable property tax payment due?

For fiscal 2027 the remaining dates are February 1, 2027 for the third quarter and May 3, 2027 for the fourth. Check your actual bill, since the Collector sets the schedule each year.

Do I need a septic inspection to sell my Barnstable house?

Normally, if the house has a septic system. Title 5 requires it, with limited exemptions such as family transfers. Timing is within two years before the sale or six months after if weather blocks it.

What is the deed excise tax in Barnstable County?

$1.50 per $500 of the price or fraction of it. Your closing attorney can work out the amount for your sale.

Attleboro at a glance

Attleboro, in Bristol County, borders Rhode Island. Its 2020 population of 46,461 is a record high, and it has 19,097 housing units, 4.4 percent of them vacant. The Providence area is its main orbit, with ties to Boston too.

Ads here tend to lead with a village name, since the city grew from old mill hamlets and crossroads: City Center beside the L.G. Balfour Riverwalk, South Attleboro near the state line, West and East Attleboro, Hebronville, Dodgeville, Maple Square, Briggs Corner, North Corner, Oak Hill, Park Square, East Junction and Camp Hebron.

Settlement dates to 1634, which means your house could be almost any age. Look over the furnace, wiring and roof before deciding what to ask.

Commuting and buyer appeal

Interstate 95 enters the state between Attleboro and Pawtucket, and Interstate 295 ends nearby. Two MBTA commuter rail stops exist, one downtown and one in South Attleboro. GATRA buses link Attleboro, Taunton and surrounding towns.

Homes close to a train stop or an I-95 ramp draw commuters headed for Providence or Boston, so say so if yours is one.

Payment schedule and methods

Payments come due on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. When one lands on a weekend or holiday, the new deadline is Monday. The collector's real estate tax page lists a few rules that catch owners off guard.

  • Late balances collect interest every day, 14 percent over a year.
  • A postmark earns no credit with the city; money must arrive on time.
  • If the bill never reached you, the tax and the interest are still owed.
  • You can pay online, by phone, through the mail, in person at City Hall (77 Park Street), or in the drop box at the Pine Street entrance.

That same page covers municipal lien certificates and tax title, so start there if you have a balance and plan to sell.

Bills after a sale

Whoever holds title on January 1 of the assessment year is the one the bill goes to. A buyer may wait a while before a bill shows their name, and the city urges new owners to check their details with the Assessor's Office.

A later bill may never reach the buyer, so square up the tax on the closing statement.

Assessor's deadlines

DateEvent or deadline
July 1Fiscal year begins; personal exemptions are judged as of this day

January 1Valuation date that sets the next fiscal year's assessment
February 1Last day to file for a property tax abatement

June 30Fiscal year closes

If the city turns down your abatement, you can appeal. The state's Appellate Tax Board guide gives you three months to take that step.

When the bill goes unpaid

Skip a payment and a lien attaches to the house immediately; a taking can come next. In the Land Court's overview describes it, thirty days of silence can trigger a demand, and a taking may be recorded 14 days later. Until a court enters a foreclosure judgment, paying the full amount owed gets the property back.

A sale inside that window pays the balance out of proceeds. Daily interest at 14 percent per year means the payoff keeps growing the longer you wait.

One and two family homes need a smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate before they sell. Deeds for Attleboro property are filed with the Bristol County Registry of Deeds. The Assessor's page links to deed searches, a quick way to see how your name appears on record.

Steps for selling with taxes owed

  2. Order a municipal lien certificate so your attorney has a firm figure.
  3. Confirm with the Assessor's Office that the owner details match your deed.

  5. At closing, your attorney pays the balance out of your proceeds.

A realistic timeline

In an Attleboro sale, city offices usually control the schedule more than the buyer does. Bills fall on quarterly dates, so ask the collector early which installment is next and whether you will owe it before closing. The fire department will not book the alarm inspection until you have a closing date, so call the day the date is fixed.

Owners who are behind face a tighter clock. The city can send a demand after 30 days of nonpayment, then record a taking 14 days after that. A buyer willing to close on your chosen date lets you clear the full amount before then.

Cash Home Buyers plans around the closing date you need. We purchase in current condition, so no repair requests get negotiated, and the lien certificate, payoff and deed recording are handled through closing with your attorney.

What to gather before you call

Start with your latest bill, your mortgage statement if a loan remains, plus any city letter about overdue amounts. If a relative owned the house before you, have the deed information handy, because the owner of record on January 1 determines who is sent the bill.

Then make two calls. The collector can give you the balance and interest so far. The Assessor's Office can verify the owner details on file and say whether an abatement application is open. Ask both offices to put any figures in writing. Note each person's name and the date you called. Bring those notes to your first talk with the attorney so nothing has to be asked twice. If you are weighing an abatement, remember the February 1 deadline and that you should keep paying while it is decided.

If the house has sat empty or needs heavy work, say so to buyers at the start. A cash buyer expects a rough house, whereas a buyer relying on a mortgage may back out after the inspection.

Listing, selling on your own, or a cash offer

Each path costs you something, and your priorities decide which cost you can live with.

A listing can bring a higher price for a well-kept property, but showings and negotiation become your burden. Going without an agent saves the commission, yet you handle the marketing and the paperwork yourself. A direct cash offer fits a house needing work, an estate sale, or an owner who needs a dependable closing date. Compare offers by what you would actually pocket after taxes, payoffs and repairs.

The 2020 census put the city at 46,461 residents, a record high.

When are Attleboro property taxes due?

Installments fall on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1, shifting to Monday when a date lands on a weekend or holiday.

Does Attleboro accept postmarks for tax payments?

No. Funds must arrive by the due date, and late balances earn interest each day at 14 percent per year.

What is the deadline for an Attleboro abatement application?

February 1 is the last day to file a property tax abatement application with the Assessor's Office.

Can I sell my Attleboro house with taxes owed?

Yes. Closing pays off taxes and liens from your proceeds, so ask the collector for a written payoff figure ahead of time.
